news.title: Team Trump Trolls Taylor Swift After 'August' Muted on Its TikTok
news.text:
Taylor Swift’s song “August” disappeared from a Team Trump TikTok video on Friday, days after the account used the track in a clip celebrating President Donald Trump and taunted the pop star in its caption.

The @TeamTrump account, which has 14 million followers and launched ahead of the 2024 election, posted the video earlier in the week using the song from Swift’s 2020 album “Folklore.” The clip showed Trump and first lady Melania Trump standing on a balcony watching fireworks, overlaid with text reading, “Mood because it’s August and Donald Trump is your president.”

The caption needled Swift directly.

“I’m sure @Taylor Swift is going to be super excited we used her song! #taylorswift #maga #august,” the account wrote.

@teamtrump I’m sure @Taylor Swift is going to be super excited we used her song! #taylorswift #maga #august ♬ som original – ⸆⸉ ོ

U.S. users noticed Friday evening that the audio had been stripped. A message on the video now reads that the copyright owner has not made the sound available. Neither Swift’s representatives nor the Trump campaign has said what caused the removal, and it remains unclear whether Swift or the rights holders for her music pulled the track.

Swift’s fans celebrated the disappearance in the comments.

“TAYLOR REMOVING THE AUDIO QUEEEEEEN,” one user wrote.

Rather than drop the exchange, Team Trump leaned in. The account posted a follow-up TikTok using a live version of Swift’s 2012 track “Red,” pairing it with mocked-up album artwork featuring Trump’s face and a fake “Red (Trump’s Version)” playlist.

“Did you know Taylor Swift wrote a whole album about the color of the Republican Party,” the post read.

The video rewrote several of Swift’s song titles to fit Republican messaging. “Everything Has Changed” became “Everything Has Changed (At Our Southern Border),” while “The Last Time” was reworked to “The Last Time (An Autopen Runs the Country).”

“August” was not the only song scrubbed from the account. Videos using Swift’s 2025 tracks “Father Figure” and “Opalite” also lost their audio, while a clip on the White House TikTok soundtracked with her song “The Fate of Ophelia” remained available.

Trump declared “I HATE TAYLOR SWIFT!” on Truth Social in 2024 and later said the pop star was “no longer hot,” after Swift endorsed Kamala Harris for president ahead of the 2024 election. A month before that endorsement, Trump shared AI-generated images falsely suggesting Swift had backed his campaign, including one portraying her as Uncle Sam.
news.summary:
Taylor Swift's song "August" disappeared from a Team Trump TikTok video on Friday, days after the account used the track in a clip celebrating President Donald Trump and taunted the pop star in its caption.

news.title: California may fine content creators who don’t disclose they were paid to post about politics
news.text:
SACRAMENTO, Calif. (AP) — Weeks before voting ended in California’s primary for governor, Los Angeles-based influencer Shaka Smith took to Instagram to tell his more than 700,000 followers whom he was voting for and why. 

“Healthcare shouldn’t bankrupt you, housing should not feel impossible, polluters shouldn’t pass their bill to us, and artists should not be replaced by AI,” Smith said. 

“That’s why I’m supporting Tom Steyer for governor.”

But Smith started the video with a disclaimer: “This is an ad, and honestly, I wish more political content said that first.” His caption specified that he was paid by Steyer’s campaign.

California is one of two states, along with Texas, that have passed policies requiring content creators to say if they’ve been paid by a political campaign to post, and the Golden State is considering cracking down by fining people who don’t.

Campaigns have long worked with celebrities and major influencers to win over voters, but now they are teaming up with smaller creators — sometimes with fewer than 100,000 followers — to reach more tailored audiences. 

That has sparked debates about whether disclosure rules for political advertisements should apply to content creators, who are expected to play prominent roles in the upcoming midterms and the 2028 presidential election.

“If you’re running for president and you are not currently trying to court some of these people or lining up your own people to act as surrogates for you, you’re already behind,” said Mike Nellis, a Democratic strategist who worked for Kamala Harris’ presidential campaign.

Questions about transparency have been fuelled by high-profile instances of influencers making content intended to change minds or votes without disclosing they were paid for it.

news.title: Joe Biden struggling with ‘painful’ cancer spread
news.text:
Former US president Joe Biden’s cancer is spreading further and causing him great pain even as he keeps up his public obligations, his son has said.

Biden, 83, was diagnosed with stage four prostate cancer in May last year, several months after leaving office.

Speaking to BBC Newsnight, his son Hunter Biden admitted it was “really sad to watch”.

“The only thing I’ll say about my dad, about his health right now, is I wish he would complain more. Because it’s not good,” Hunter Biden said.

“The cancer has spread, mestastasised, into his bones and further.

“It’s very painful, and it’s very debilitating in many respects.”

However, he said, his father remained publicly active.

“But he’s still out there, he’s still doing his thing … he so believes in this country,” Hunter Biden said.

Joe Biden’s age was a key factor in his decision to abruptly withdraw from the 2024 presidential campaign, after concerns grew within the Democratic Party about his mental and physical stamina.

A disastrous debate against Republican candidate Donald Trump, during which Biden appeared forgetful and exhausted, was the final catalyst for him to pull out of the campaign, on which the Democrats approved the candidacy of Vice President Kamala Harris.

Biden was the oldest president in US history, but will be surpassed by current White House occupant Trump before the end of Trump’s second term.

Trump’s own onstage gaffes and misstatements, such as a recent reference to “the Islamic Republic of Japan”, have also drawn some speculation as to his mental wellbeing, but Trump’s meandering dialogue is more consistent with his long-term public speaking pattern.

Both men received approving fitness reports during their time as president, though Trump has made several visits to Walter Reed medical centre in his second term.

His administration has insisted those visits, which have included cognitive tests, are mere routine.

Hunter Biden, himself the target of attacks from the Republican Party in an attempt to link his father to alleged shady business dealings, has recently emerged as a social media star, following years of drug addiction and scandal.

The younger Biden has embraced his past baggage and his recovery, and has launched frequent attacks on the Trump administration, such as a recent sardonic congratulatory message to the president for the record number of times he had ended the Iran war.
news.author: Adam Vidler

news.title: Joe Biden's cancer has spread beyond bones and is ‘very painful', says son
news.text:
Former US President Joe Biden’s prostate cancer has spread beyond his bones and is causing him significant pain, his son Hunter Biden said in an interview with the BBC.

“The cancer has spread, metastasised into his bones and further,” Hunter Biden told BBC’s Newsnight, according to video posted online on Friday. “It’s very painful, and it’s very debilitating in many respects.”

Hunter Biden became emotional while discussing his father’s condition.

“It’s really, really hard, and it’s really sad to watch,” he said, adding that his father remained active and committed to the United States.

A spokesman for the 83-year-old Biden declined to comment on the interview on Saturday.

Biden revealed in May 2025, less than four months after leaving the White House, that he had been diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer that had already spread to his bones.

He later underwent radiation and hormone therapy. Last month, while announcing his forthcoming memoir, Biden said his treatment was going “really well”.

Biden’s health had been closely scrutinised during his presidency, particularly after his poor performance in a June 2024 debate against Donald Trump. Biden withdrew from the presidential race following pressure from fellow Democrats, and Vice President Kamala Harris became the Democratic nominee. Trump went on to defeat Harris in the November election.

Biden, who served as president from 2021 to 2025, was the oldest person to win the US presidency when he was elected in 2020. He had previously served as Barack Obama’s vice president from 2009 to 2017.

Despite his illness, Biden has continued to make public appearances. He attended the dedication of Obama’s presidential library in Chicago in June.

His presidential memoir is scheduled for release on November 17.

news.title: Taylor Swift Silences Trump's TikTok After He Used Her Song Without Asking
news.text: On Monday, the "Team Trump" TikTok account posted a clip showing President Trump and First Lady Melania watching a July Fourth fireworks show from a balcony. The footage was set to "August," a track off Swift's 2020 album "Folklore," and fans quickly pointed out how stiff and awkward the pair looked standing there. The caption that went along with the post joked that Swift would be thrilled her music had been used, tagging both her name and the hashtag maga. Fans Demand Swift Step InIt didn't take long for Swift's fanbase to react. Commenters flooded the post calling on the singer to get the song taken down, with one early comment predicting she'd intervene racking up close to 25,000 likes on its own. Swift never said anything publicly about the video. But based on what happened next, it looks like she or someone working with her took action behind the scenes. The Audio Goes SilentBy Friday evening, the clip had changed. The song was gone, replaced by total silence and a label reading that the audio was no longer available. The timing made the whole thing even more awkward, since the original caption bragging about Swift's supposed excitement was still sitting right there, untouched. Fans had a field day with the reversal. One person cheered Swift on for muting the track, while another joked about whether the song was still around at all. A third commenter said Trump's team had picked the wrong woman to mess with, and a fourth simply congratulated Swift for getting it done. As of Saturday, Team Trump still had not updated or removed the original caption, leaving the now silent video and its outdated joke online for everyone to see. A Feud With HistoryThis isn't the first run in between Trump and Swift. Back in 2020, after years of Trump publicly praising her, Swift turned on him in a pointed post on social media, accusing him of stoking racism throughout his presidency and calling out his rhetoric around violence, before urging her followers to vote him out that November. Things escalated further in 2024 when Swift, known as the highest grossing live performer in the world, endorsed Kamala Harris. Trump did not take it well, declaring on social media that he hated her. He kept the jabs going into his return to the White House, questioning out loud whether Swift had somehow become less popular ever since he said he hated her.
news.summary: Fans are celebrating after Taylor Swift appears to have had her song "August" pulled from a Trump campaign TikTok that used it without permission.
news.author: Sagar Kar

news.title: Taylor Swift songs removed from several White House TikTok videos
news.text:
Taylor Swift's music is no longer available on several videos posted by President Donald Trump's Team Trump TikTok page.

An Aug. 3 edited video showing the president and first lady Melania Trump watching fireworks featured text reading "mood because it's August and Donald Trump is your president" while the caption read "I’m sure @Taylor Swift is going to be super excited we used her song! #taylorswift #maga #august." The video originally included her hit 2020 track "August," off the superstar singer's "Folklore" album, but no sound is available now.

The comments celebrated the removal of the music, writing "TAYLOR REMOVING THE AUDIO QUEEEEEEN," while another reads, "Sorry, what was that? cant hear the song."

Several videos that featured Swift songs on the Team Trump TikTok account now have no audio, including one from November that used her "Life of a Showgirl" track "Father Figure" while honoring the president in a video montage.

USA TODAY has reached out to the White House and Swift's representatives for comment.

Trump page says Taylor Swift wrote 'Red' about Republicans

Another Team Trump video to lose its audio was one from Aug. 6 where the page quips that the Grammy-winning artist wrote her fourth studio album "Red" about Republicans. The video, now soundless, displays artwork imitating the "Red" album cover but with Trump wearing a red MAGA hat with the text "Red (Donald Trump's version)."

"Did you know Taylor Swift wrote a whole album about the color of the Republican Party?" the video asks.

Swift previously endorsed former Vice President Kamala Harris, the Democratic frontrunner against Trump, ahead of the 2024 presidential election. Days later, Trump declared on TruthSocial, "I hate Taylor Swift," and in May 2025, the president declared that "she's no longer HOT" since he said he hated her.

However, following the singer-songwriter's engagement to now-husband Travis Kelce in August 2025, Trump said, "Well, I wish them a lot of luck. I think he's a great player, a great guy. I think she's a terrific person" in a Cabinet meeting when asked by a reporter.

Several pop stars have condemned White House over song use

The White House has seemingly leaned into rage-baiting musicians who have not endorsed the Trump administration by playing their music on social media, prompting several artists to clap back publicly.

A July 23 video showing U.S. military strikes in Iran shared by the White House's official TikTok page featured Katy Perry's 2010 track "Firework." The pop star said she was "deeply appalled and angry," clarifying that she "did not approve this, I was not asked, and I absolutely do not condone it."

"I wrote this song to be an anthem of hope, healing, and inner strength for people going through their darkest personal moments. To see a message of self-worth and upliftment weaponized to soundtrack destruction and violence is a complete violation of everything my song stands for," she wrote in a July 25 post on X. "My music is for bringing people together, not celebrating warfare."

Ariana Grande commented under a June 9 TikTok video posted by the White House depicting federal agents arresting and handcuffing people while featuring her 2024 song "Bye," according to reports by Reuters and The Guardian.

"Please do not ever use my music in relation to this barbaric, inhumane, heinous nonsense," she wrote. The audio and Grande's comment were later removed.

Kesha, Olivia Rodrigo, Noah Kahan and Sabrina Carpenter have also slammed the White House's use of their songs for different videos without their permission.

In response to Kahan condemning the account's use of his music, the page posted a July 31 video with text reading "And for that reason we will be posting Noah Kahan music."

news.title: Taylor Swift song ‘August’ removed from Trump TikTok
news.text:
A TikTok video posted by Donald Trump’s campaign that included Taylor Swift’s song “August” has had the sound removed since it was posted four days ago.

The TikTok account @TeamTrump shared a video soundtracked to the song, depicting Donald and Melania Trump standing on a balcony watching fireworks with the text: “Mood because it’s August and Donald Trump is your president.”

The caption reads: “I’m sure @Taylor Swift is going to be super excited we used her song! #taylorswift #maga #august.”

Fans noticed Friday that Swift’s track, from her 2020 album Folklore, has since been removed from the post by the copyright owner.

In the U.S. version of the TikTok app, a message on the video reads: “The copyright owner hasn’t made this sound available in your country.” 

After the song was stripped from the post, one of Swift’s fans showed support by commenting: “TAYLOR REMOVING THE AUDIO QUEEEEEEN.”

“Is the song with us right now?” said another.

The Independent has contacted representatives for Swift and Trump for comment.

The Team Trump TikTok account, which has 14 million followers, was created ahead of the 2024 U.S. presidential election. 

A video posted by the account in November that included Swift’s song “Father Figure” has also had the audio removed. 

The Team Trump account has appeared to troll Swift further, posting a screenshot of the tracklist for Swift’s album Red, but with the text and images altered in favor of Trump.

The album’s title was changed to Red (Donald Trump’s Version) while song titles included “Red (Taylor Swift Wrote A Whole Album About Republicans)” and “We Are Never Ever Getting Back Together (The Biden Harris Administration).”

It is not the first time the Trump administration has made a public dig at the world-renowned singer. On her July 4th wedding day, the White House issued a social media post parodying the billboards that were displayed in Manhattan’s Midtown announcing that the singer and Travis Kelce had tied the knot at Madison Square Garden.

“IT’S HAPPENED!!!” the White House’s official X account said in a post, along with an AI-generated picture of pink billboards saying, “Trump is your president.”

Trump and Swift have had bad blood for years. The feud escalated in 2024 after Swift endorsed Trump’s opponent Kamala Harris for president by saying, “I think she is a steady-handed, gifted leader and I believe we can accomplish so much more in this country if we are led by calm and not chaos.”

The endorsement enraged Trump and caused him to write on social media: “I HATE TAYLOR SWIFT!”

He went on to warn that Swift would “pay a price for it in the marketplace.”

In 2025, he mocked her again on his platform by writing, “Has anyone noticed that, since I said ‘I HATE TAYLOR SWIFT,’ she’s no longer ‘HOT?’”

However, he seemed to cool off later in the year. When news of Swift and Kelce’s engagement was announced in August, Trump congratulated the couple while speaking to reporters at a cabinet meeting.

“Well, I wish them a lot of luck,” Trump said. “I think it’s — I think he’s a great player, I think he’s a great guy and I think that she’s a terrific person. So I wish them a lot of luck.”
news.summary: The president has made public digs at the ‘Love Story’ singer for years

news.title: California may fine content creators who don't disclose they were paid to post about politics
news.text:
Campaigns have long worked with celebrities and major influencers to win over voters, but now they are teaming up with smaller creators - sometimes with fewer than 100,000 followers - to reach more tailored audiences. That has sparked debates about whether disclosure rules for political advertisements should apply to content creators, who are expected to play prominent roles in the upcoming midterms and the 2028 presidential election.

"If you're running for president and you are not currently trying to court some of these people or lining up your own people to act as surrogates for you, you're already behind," said Mike Nellis, a Democratic strategist who worked for Kamala Harris' presidential campaign.

Questions about transparency have been fueled by high-profile instances of influencers making content intended to change minds or votes without disclosing they were paid for it.

In 2022, the campaign of then-Senate candidate John Fetterman paid Nicole "Snooki" Polizzi of "Jersey Shore" to record a video teasing his GOP rival for leaving New Jersey before announcing his run in Pennsylvania. In 2023, content creators were paid by an influencer marketing agency with conservative ties to defend Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, a Republican, after he was impeached for alleged bribery and other accusations of misconduct, according to the Texas Tribune. The payments weren't clearly disclosed in either case.

Steyer, a Democratic billionaire who spent more than $215 million of his own money in his unsuccessful bid for governor, took fire from rivals for paying content creators. He wasn't the only hopeful in the race paying influencers, but he faced much of the blowback since he'd already been accused of trying to buy the election. Many of the creators who worked with Steyer's campaign disclosed that they were paid, but the state's campaign finance watchdog is investigating several other instances in which creators allegedly didn't.

news.title: Muturi: Why I disagree with Gachagua's political approach
news.text:
Democratic Party (DP)leader Justin Muturi has elaborated why he is opposed to Democracy for Citizens Party (DCP) leader Rigathi Gachagua on several issues, such as the formula to identify a Presidential candidate and his calls to invite political parties around Mt Kenya with a view to forming a coalition.
Muturi has also reiterated his earlier condemnation of Gachagua’s remarks, where he has repeatedly claimed that the Mt Kenya region was behind the DCP party, saying the remarks appeared to suggest that other political parties had no say in the negotiation table.
In an exclusive interview with The Sunday Standard, Muturi said his decision and those of other party leaders, including Peter Munya (PNU), Lenny Kivuti) Development Empowerment Party (DEP) was informed by Gachagua’s claims on July 26 at a function in the Catholic Church in Imenti Central where he reportedly urged four political parties to fold.

“I personally read that story on Monday 27th, and I thought, first of all, it was a mistake; it's a misreporting. I decided I'm not going to comment on it, but I was waiting and hoping that maybe Gachagua or somebody from his party who was present with him on that occasion would perhaps correct or even call me, reach out to me and tell me that what is reported is not correct,” he said.
According to Muturi, it was him who reached out to his colleagues after he was informed by an aspirant from Kawira Mwangaza’s Umoja na Maendeleo Party (UMP) who reportedly informed him that she had been informed by Gachagua’s orderlies that she was popular but in a wrong political party, remarks Muturi interpreted to be undermining of other parties within the Opposition.
“The lady felt extremely embarrassed, and when those stories started coming up, we thought, this is not right. The country, as we all know, is a multi-party democratic state. We have always had many parties in the country. In fact, today, I think there could be close to a hundred or more than a hundred.”
He added, “Why would anybody single out our four parties to dissolve and join him? We thought it was a bad taste, and therefore it was necessary to call him out and tell him that coalitions are very sensitive. People must always be sensitive to what they say because you may be saying something lightly, but it could have far-reaching consequences and ramifications,’ he said.
He said he saw no reason to reach out to Gachagua since it was him who first framed the story and that he was obligated to reach out to his colleagues to set the record straight.
“I thought I would give him that period because it was something which was reported widely in the newspapers and for me to reach out to him, I think I would be lowering my dignity. It was him who framed the story because if he said it, then it was reported as he said it, but if that's not what he said, after seeing it, it would be helpful to reach out to us to say, no, what has been reported is not correct,” he said.
He added that Gachagua, on many occasions, had failed to recognize his presence in public rallies.
Additionally, Muturi categorically opposed Gachagua’s calls where he urged him to convene a meeting for all the political parties within Mt Kenya and possibly form an alliance dubbed Hyena’s coalition, maintaining that the Opposition leaders ought to focus on establishing a national political alliance and not a village one.
“I lead a party, he leads a party, and actually one of the things that he said is that all those parties will be at liberty to field candidates for all the other positions. Parties in the Mt Kenya region are just a part of the various parties in Kenya. They're 32, you can imagine; if you start summoning all the parties, you'll find yourself mixing leopards and goats. So we have to be very careful,” Muturi said.
He said Gachagua’s proposal could not augur well for democracy, saying it should suffice that every party is at liberty to conduct individual campaigns, adding that ‘I think it is not even necessary.’
On Gachagua’s position that the Opposition should wait until the homestretch, Muturi said adhering to his proposal would give President William Ruto a win on a silver platter, saying they would not get time to meet the strict timelines laid out by the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC).
He explained that the proposal to name the Presidential candidate by May would work against the Opposition since it would coincide with the timelines for the Presidential candidates to submit their nomination papers to the electoral agency and must have collected 2000 signatures in not less than 24 counties.
“Now, if we wait until that time, it means that all of us who have declared interest then will not be ready. We have to begin moving, getting 2,000 signatures in no less than 24 counties, all of us. So it means that all of us then must set up secretariats working exclusively for ourselves, not for the joint candidate. If we delay the decision of the presidential flag bearer, we run the risk of being unprepared.
Muturi said hurried decisions were to blame for the Democratic Party loss in the United States election in 2024 following its decision to replace former President Joe Biden with Kamala Harris and the 2016 loss after the party took time to decide who between Bernie Sanders and Hillary Clinton would be the party’s Presidential candidate.
He added that the 2002 moment in Kenya’s Presidential election that Gachagua referred to while justifying his reasoning of not naming their Presidential candidate could not be equated with the next year’s general election.
Gachagua had maintained that Mwai Kibaki was named the Opposition’s flagbearer two months before the election saying there was no hurry to name their candidate.
However, Muturi said the dynamics had changed as the election would be held under the timelines of the 2010 Constitution, which was not in place and which stated about 50 plus one per cent for a Presidential candidate to be declared a winner.
“At that time, the constitution did not require 50 plus 1. It did not require 25% in at least 24 counties. All it required was first past the post which is the reason why the second President Daniel Moi had been winning against his disjointed opposition. Because it didn't matter that even in 1992 and 1997, the combined votes by the individual opposition presidential candidates put together were about twice what Moi used to get through.
He added, “We have the 2010 constitution. It has its own peculiar and stringent requirements. So when you tell me that we can name a presidential candidate running it in May, then you don't know what it entails. Some of us have been involved in these campaigns. We need teams and think tanks, working on a common agenda of a new government, a new administration, that will give confidence to the people. That will address the issue of rule of law, constitutionalism, independence of institutions, and the economy.
He said failing to move first and name a Presidential candidate by this year meant giving Ruto the victory on a silver platter and said if the Opposition waited until May, he would not participate in the campaigns.
“If we wait until May, I can assure you, I think I will not even bother to participate because we will have given him a victory on a silver platter. We are going to have over 55,000 polling stations in the 2027 general election. Even on the bare minimum, that means you must have not less than 110,000 agents. You are not just going to pick people whom you have not interacted with,” Muturi maintained.
He said agents were a critical pillar in the Presidential elections and identifying them early was key to reducing the risks of using double agents to work for the interests of rival political formations.
“It was shown here in the recent Olkalou by-election. The constituency has 144 polling stations, meaning the Jubilee Party had 288 agents but the candidate got 198 votes, meaning some of the agents did not even vote for their candidate.
"All these will look simple, but you can imagine if you multiply that throughout the republic; 110,000 agents is just a bare minimum. Those people, you need to have meetings with them, and the teams will need to move from Nairobi, go to the various regions, have meetings with these people, create rapport, and build confidence among them. That will not happen if you wait until May,” he said.
According to Muturi, the justification that naming the Presidential candidate could expose him or her to unwarranted attacks by the government do not hold water, saying nothing prevented the President from saying or doing anything to the Opposition leaders.
“Who doesn't Ruto know? We knew Ruto was going to run for president in 2013. After 10 years. The late Raila Odinga, Kalonzo Musyoka, Moses Wetangula, Musalia Mudavadi, they knew that the person they were going to face in 2022 was going to be Ruto,” he observed.
Despite Muturi’s ideological differences with Gachagua, Muturi described him as humble, listening and reasonable while appearing in closed-door meetings, and that the character disappears during his public engagements.
“When we are together, Rigathi is a very humble man behind the camera. I think the cameras excite him; I think you people, and then the crowds, excite him, but he's a very humble man. We have had several meetings quietly; he's not the kind of, that overbearing,” he said.
“You sit down with Rigathi, and you discuss things, and he's reasonable. He will state his position, his point of view, which is very democratic, and everybody else is at liberty even to contradict him; in fact, you can never even hear him raise his voice over what other people's suggestions are, but cameras make him get some other things, and then he forgets that he has other colleagues.”
He, however, maintained that the Opposition leaders were working together with the common goal of unseating Ruto in next year’s elections, saying the Principals would meet yesterday for consultations.
“Two weeks ago I was in Nanyuki opening my party office and meeting people and later did my public rallies around Nanyuki town. The other weekend on the 16th, I will be opening my party branch office in Muranga. You saw Fred Matianyi was busy in Nyamira; Gachagua was in Kajiado yesterday to receive MCAs from Wiper,” he added. 
He said on 22nd of this month, the Opposition will conduct a joint rally in Busia and Trans Nzoia and later attend a memorial service of the former Vice President Kijana Wamalwa.
While addressing the objection by a section of Opposition leaders to join the Azimio coalition, Muturi, who is among the key leaders who are in the process of rebranding the coalition’s Constitution, said they would review the deed of agreement and change some of the contentious issues to accommodate all parties.
“We are talking about reconstitution and rebranding. Those are some of the things that people can place on the table and say look, this puts you in an advantageous position relative to ourselves, and then we can discuss. Everything is out for debate and agreed upon,” he added.
Some of the leaders within the Opposition, such as People’s Liberation Party (PLP) leader Martha Karua, whose party exited the Azimio coalition, and Gachagua have openly resisted calls to join the coalition, suggesting that they needed to form a new coalition party.
He remained upbeat that with a clear strategy on a road map to next year’s election, the Opposition would oust the Kenya Kwanza administration even as he dismissed Deputy President Kithure Kindiki’s calls to court him, Kivuti and Munya back to the government.
“I am never interested in working with Ruto. Kindiki has forgotten that before leaving government, I had written three letters to Ruto telling him, if you do not, in cabinet, have an agenda on extrajudicial killings, abductions, I will never attend a cabinet meeting of your government. Kindiki must be having a short memory.
He added, “If we can't remove Ruto, I don't want a job, not in his government, and I'm comfortable; I'm okay to stay without a job,” he added.
He claimed Kindiki had no moral obligation to unite the Mt Kenya region since he was allegedly involved in a legal battle to delink the Tharaka community from the Meru community.
He was referring to a court battle that saw the Tharaka community officially delinked and recognized as a distinct tribe separate from the Meru community during the 2019 Kenya Population and Housing Census data compilation, following historical pushes for independent identity.
“Kindiki went to court himself in 2016 and filed a case to declare the Tharakas as non-Merus, and that is why in the census of 2019, the Tharakas were counted separately from Merus. That is why today, he has a problem going to Meru. Why does he want to benefit from Meru? He posed.

news.title: Joe Biden’s cancer is spreading to other parts of his body, Hunter says
news.text:
Former President Joe Biden’s cancer continues to worsen, according to his son Hunter Biden.

“The cancer has spread, metastasized into his bones and further,” he said of his father in a Friday interview with the BBC. “It's very painful. It’s very debilitating in many respects, but he’s still out there. He’s still doing his thing. He so believes in this country.”

“It’s really, really hard and it’s really sad to watch,” Biden added of how the former president’s struggles have impacted the family. 

In an interview this month with SiriusXM’s Let’s Talk Off Camera with Kelly Ripa, former First Lady Dr. Jill Biden spoke of the president’s “challenging” prostate cancer diagnosis, which he announced last May.

“We have to be mindful of it every three months, testing and medicines,” she said. “And anybody who’s gone through this cancer journey — and I’ve been through it many times with members of my family, of course with Beau — it’s constant. It’s daily. And I think it’s challenging.”

The former president’s eldest son, Beau, died from glioblastoma, an aggressive form of brain cancer, in 2015.

Last month, as the former president announced a forthcoming memoir, he said his treatment had been progressing positively.

"I’ve been spending a lot of time with my family,” he said in a statement. “I’m dealing with a cancer diagnosis, been getting treatment, and it’s going really well. I want to thank all those who have offered their prayers and support and well-wishes. It’s meant the world to me and to Jill."

Last May, the Democrat announced he had been diagnosed with an “aggressive” form of prostate cancer. He has subsequently been undergoing radiation and hormone therapy, according to his office.

Concern over Biden’s health and mental fitness dominated the end of his second term and 2024 presidential campaign, from which he ultimately dropped out, clearing the way for his Vice President Kamala Harris to mount an unsuccessful bid for the White House against Donald Trump. 

Critics accused the Biden administration of concealing the extent of the president’s health struggles and paving the way for the Democrats’ bruising 2024 loss.

Since leaving office, Biden has largely kept with the presidential tradition of remaining quiet about his successor, though he hit out at Trump in June during a Democratic fundraiser in Maryland, calling the Republican a “loser” for continuing to pursue “vanity projects” such as demolishing the East Wing of the White House to build a ballroom.

The ex-president has a endorsed a handful of candidates ahead of the midterms, where Democrats are forecast to retake the House with the balance of power in Congress at stake.

Overall, it appears both the former president and Democrats on the ballot are not trying to bring too much attention to the Biden administration after leaving office with a poor approval rating circling the high 30s. 

In an election season dominated by affordability concerns, some ex-Biden officials have made a point of not mentioning the Democrat in their campaign, perhaps owing to Biden’s association with high inflation towards the end of his term.

Meanwhile, Biden’s memoir, Promise Me, America, will not come out until after the midterms. 

Throughout this year, health concerns about aging lawmakers have been a major topic of conversation in Washington D.C. following the sudden death of Sen. Lindsey Graham and the extended hospitalization of Sen. Mitch McConnell, who was discharged from a rehabilitation center this Thursday after missing weeks of congressional business.
news.summary: The former president was diagnosed with an ‘aggressive’ form of prostate cancer last May

news.title: Team Trump TikTok Targets Taylor Swift Again in Viral Jab
news.text:
President Donald Trump’s social media team appeared to needle Taylor Swift after a track by the pop superstar was reportedly pulled from the campaign’s TikTok account.

In response, Trump’s TikTok operation posted a fresh video featuring Swift’s song Red, the title track from her 2012 album.

The clip included a spoof version of the album artwork, swapping Swift’s close-up image and trademark red lipstick for a photo of Trump in his familiar red MAGA cap, alongside a fake playlist titled “Red (Donald Trump’s Version).”

“Did you know Taylor Swift wrote a whole album about the color of the Republican Party,” the post teased.

By midday Saturday, however, the Red audio had also disappeared from Team Trump’s TikTok page, apparently removed by Swift, 36, or someone representing her. A notice on the platform stated: “This sound isn’t available.”

The Daily Mail has contacted representatives for both Swift and the White House for comment, but neither had responded at the time of publication.

The latest back-and-forth over Swift’s music follows reports that the singer, whose new husband was recently criticized over his “dad bod,” allegedly blocked a Team Trump TikTok video that used her song august.

The trolling White House clip that was posted four days ago showed the backs of Trump, 80, who said he ‘hates’ Swift, and First Lady Melania Trump, 56, as they watched fireworks light up the night sky.

The text appearing on the image read: ‘Mood because it’s August and Donald Trump is your president.’

Swift’s song august initially played on the soundtrack, and at the bottom of the post was a message from Team Trump saying: ‘I’m sure @Taylor Swift is going to be super excited we used her song!’ along with the hashtags #taylorswift #maga #august.

By Friday night, the audio was gone and replaced with a message that said: ‘The copyright owner hasn’t made this sound available in your country,’ and which just shouted Swift, whose ‘fairytale’ wedding left some guests ‘weirded out.’

The song august is from the singer–songwriter’s 2020 Folklore album. It’s a bittersweet track about a delicate and fleeting summer romance told from the perspective of a fictional teenage girl named Augustine. 

Swift’s fans rejoiced in the comments with one writing: ‘TAYLOR REMOVING THE AUDIO QUEEEEEEN.’ Another echoed: ‘TAYLOR QUEEN SWIFT.’

A third applauded the singer’s actions by saying: ‘TAYLOR REMOVED THE SOUND HAHAHA,’ and a fourth chimed in: ‘She removed it, clocked you guys.’

And yet another Swiftie couldn’t resist teasing: ‘Hahahahaha you messed with the wrong successful woman,’ followed by the taunting words of another fan: ‘I hope taylor swift sues you and wins.’

Swift now owns the copyright of all her songs and recordings, including august and Red. 

She officially regained ownership of her original master recordings in May 2025 after a six-year battle.

This isn’t the first time Team Trump has borrowed a Swift track for its TikTok account. In November of last year, a video included the singer’s song Father Figure, which was also removed.

But another clip added in November plugging the president still includes Swift’s The Fate of Ophelia on its audio track. 

Friction between Trump and Swift began in October 2018 when the pop star endorsed Democratic candidates in Tennessee, prompting Trump to remark he liked her music ’25 percent less.’

But their hostile feud really erupted in September 2024 after Swift publicly endorsed Kamala Harris for president. 

‘I’m voting for @kamalaharris because she fights for the rights and causes I believe need a warrior to champion them,’ she wrote on Instagram.

Trump swiftly retaliated on his Truth Social account, posting: ‘I HATE TAYLOR SWIFT!’

The POTUS took a softer stance when responding to news of Swift’s engagement to Kansas City Chiefs tight end Travis Kelce in August 2025. 

He stated that he wished them ‘a lot of luck,’ calling Kelce a ‘great player’ and Swift a ‘terrific person,’ despite their ongoing political discord.

But last month, minutes after Madison Square Garden’s billboard lit up with ‘JUST&T MARRIED,’ announcing Swift and Kelce had tied the knot, the official White House social media accounts on X and Instagram shared an AI-generated image with ‘TRUMP IS YOUR PRESIDENT’ alongside the caption: ‘IT’S HAPPENED!!!’

news.title: Cancel culture fired Shane Gillis — America hired him back
news.text:
In July, Shane Gillis made comedy history, selling more than 77,000 tickets and setting records for the largest audience for a comedian and the most tickets sold for a solo stand-up act. The achievement put him past names like Kevin Hart, Steve Martin, and German stand-up Mario Barth.

It also came just seven years after cancel culture nearly killed his career.

Shane Gillis did not beat cancel culture by becoming less offensive. He beat it by becoming too successful to cancel.

In 2019, shortly after Comedy Central named him an “Up Next” comedian, Gillis landed the job every comic dreams about: a spot on “Saturday Night Live.” Then old clips surfaced of him doing a mock Asian accent and using a racial slur. Other clips featured supposedly unacceptable jokes about gay people. Within days, SNL fired him. Gillis later described the experience as painful enough to make it hard to “trust people ... for a while.”

The timing was brutal. Gillis was fired during what we now recognize as peak woke, when careers could vanish because somebody with a Twitter account dug through 10 years of jokes and found the wrong sentence.

He was hardly alone. Sarah Silverman faced backlash over an old blackface bit. Dave Chappelle was attacked for mocking Michael Jackson’s accusers. Kevin Hart’s old tweets were dragged back into the spotlight. Suddenly the internet had discovered a tremendous new power: If enough people pretended to be offended at once, they could get somebody fired.

For a while, almost everyone played along.

That was always the secret of cancel culture. It was never a magical force. It was a consensual ideology. It worked because institutions submitted to it, employers feared it, and ordinary people convinced themselves that refusing to obey would make them the next target.

Words became temporarily unsayable. Leftists rewrote definitions and then declared that only certain people were allowed to use them. “Gone with the Wind” was pulled from streaming. James Gunn and Gina Carano lost jobs. People learned to keep their mouths shut because being called racist, sexist, or homophobic could cost them a career.

The woke mob did not win because everyone agreed with it. It won because too many people were afraid to laugh at it.

Now, two presidencies removed from peak woke, the whole thing looks much sillier. Plenty of celebrities once declared untouchable have returned to the mainstream. Land acknowledgments and pronoun rituals have become punch lines. “Culturally insensitive,” the kind of phrase that helped sink Gillis, sounds increasingly like a relic from a very stupid age.

So people post offensive jokes, recycle old podcast clips, and celebrate that “woke is dead.”

I would not start planning the funeral.

Cancel culture isn’t dead. It’s hiding.

Conservatives have every reason to feel confident right now. Republicans control Congress and the presidency. The administration has attacked “diversity, equity, and inclusion” throughout the federal government. The Supreme Court has handed down major victories protecting women’s sports. It can be tempting to believe the culture could never slide back to 2019.

RELATED: BILL PILLED: Maher warns fellow Democrats that they're headed for woke-tastrophe

 Shannon Finney/WireImage/Getty Images

But Donald Trump was president in 2019 too.

The first and second Trump administrations are very different, but Trump’s presence by itself does not prevent a woke resurgence. Cultural power does not live only in Washington. It lives in entertainment, universities, corporations, HR departments, newsrooms, and the countless people who decide whether the mob gets rewarded for showing up.

Gillis’ comeback is encouraging precisely because he did not wait for those institutions to forgive him.

Podcasts gave him somewhere else to go. After SNL fired him, Gillis joked that he could just appear on Joe Rogan’s podcast and everything would be fine. And he was right. Audiences increasingly learned that independently produced shows could be funnier, more honest, and less filtered than legacy television.

That shift reached well beyond comedy. Podcasts became a major force in the 2024 election. Trump and JD Vance used long-form appearances to show voters their humor and personalities outside carefully managed television interviews. Kamala Harris’ refusal to sit down with Rogan only reinforced the contrast. In the peak-woke era, scripted liberal slogans might have been enough. By 2024, they sounded canned.

Comedy is often the canary in the coal mine because comedy requires tension, risk, and the possibility that somebody will be offended. A culture that cannot tolerate a joke will eventually struggle to tolerate an argument.

Gillis rebuilt his career, but comedians are still testing the limits. Jerry Seinfeld said the “extreme left has suppressed the art of comedy,” then later walked that back by saying culture moves and a comedian’s job is to adapt. David Spade criticized L.A. Mayor Karen Bass and California Gov. Gavin Newsom for “killing Hollywood” and took heat for it. Nate Bargatze was slammed simply for attending Trump’s UFC event at the White House.

RELATED: Colorado fire department employee FIRED over Snoop Dogg doll that ‘evoked’ history of ‘racial terror’

 Heidi Gutman/Bravo/Getty Images

That is what hiding looks like. The old cultural reflex is still there, waiting for institutions to become afraid again.

Woke politics will not return because somebody waves a magic wand. It will return one concession at a time: one employee fired to stop a controversy, one joke declared beyond the pale, one institution deciding it is easier to surrender than tell an angry mob no.

That is why conservatives should resist the temptation to declare victory and go home. Free speech survives only when people keep using it. Comedy survives only when comedians keep telling the joke. Culture stays open only when institutions refuse to hand professional hecklers a veto.

The late, great Norm Macdonald understood this better than most. Early in his career, he joked: “People were beginning to talk about me, and that’s always good news. As Adolf Hitler once said, all publicity is good publicity.”

Shane Gillis did not beat cancel culture by becoming less offensive. He beat it by becoming too successful to cancel. That’s worth celebrating. It is not a reason to stop paying attention.

news.title: Trump triggers MAGA rage-fest with on-point take-down of his own 'dead' bill
news.text:
President Donald Trump, missing in action Saturday after the Senate confirmed his former criminal lawyer as attorney general but rendered his voting bill "effectively dead," quietly emerged to platform an on-point takedown of his beloved legislation. 

Trump, without comment, quietly shared video on Truth Social of former Vice President Kamala Harris, his Democratic rival in the 2024 presidential election, explaining her serious reservations with the SAVE America Act. 

"They're trying to mess with your ability to vote," said Harris. "You're going to have to have proof of who you are through a passport, which a lot of Americans don't have, or a birth certificate — same point."

Harris concluded Trump merely wanted to create "obstacles" to make it difficult for Americans to vote. 

Trump's followers rewarded this offering with vitriol against "crumby communists" and "cheating Commiecrats" — which might have been what wanted after the Senate abandoned the bill to go off on vacation. 

Bloomberg reporter Steven Dennis wrote on X Saturday that the SAVE America Act was "effectively dead for the midterm elections."

The SAVE America Act — which would require states to force voters to confirm U.S. citizenship when participating in elections — has been described by legal experts as redundant and dystopian. 

What's more, Trump's relentless push to see it pass infuriated members of his own party in the Senate. 

White House demands that Majority Leader Sen. John Thune (R-SD) do more to pass it outraged the majority leader and his allies. 

"This idea that he can just command members of the Republican conference to get in line is just a fantasy," Sen. John Cornyn (R-TX) said earlier this month. “It’s creating a circular firing squad for Republicans.”

But Trump's so-called "fantasy" appeared to be alive and well on Truth Social Saturday. 

"You would think Democrats would work together for a cure for stupidity," wrote one user. "But 'stupidity' just might be a major requirement to be a Democrat..."

"I guess people who agree with her think, most Americans are too stupid or ill-equipped to prove their citizenship," one of Trump's repliers wrote the president. "Once again, THEY THINK YOU ARE STUPID!!!

news.title: Can Progressive Jarrett Keohokalole Win Hawaii Primary? Final Polls
news.text: Hawaii voters are heading to the polls Saturday in a Democratic primary for the state's 1st Congressional District that has emerged as a high-stakes test of the party's internal divide over experience versus generational change. Representative Ed Case, a 73-year-old moderate incumbent who has spent much of the past two decades in Washington, faces a robust challenge from 43-year-old state Senator Jarrett Keohokalole. The contest mirrors progressive primary challenges nationwide targeting veteran lawmakers whom critics view as out of step with the party's grassroots base. What Final Polls Show Polling data ahead of Election Day paints a picture of a competitive race, though entering with contrasting momentum. Prediction Edge averages from surveys conducted between October 2025 and July 2026 showed Case leading the field with 39.8 percent support, followed by Keohokalole at 27.3 percent and former state House Speaker Della Au Belatti at 21 percent. However, Belatti announced in May that she was giving up her bid for Congress to run for lieutenant governor. The New York Times' polling tracker similarly showed Case ahead but not out of danger. A poll by Blueprint Polling on July 24 shows Keohokalole leading Case, 47 percent to 38 percent among 278 likely voters. However, in a survey from Blueprint Polling that was conducted between July 7-8, Case was ahead by 8 points—33 percent to 25 percent. Both polls were sponsored by Keohokalole. Prediction markets also pointed to a much tighter race than the polling averages alone. As of early Saturday afternoon, Prediction Edge showed Case with a 56 percent chance of winning the nomination compared with 48 percent for Keohokalole. Establishment vs. Progressive The campaign has largely focused on competing visions of leadership for the safely Democratic, Honolulu-based district. Case won reelection in 2024 with about 72 percent of the vote while Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris received about 62 percent of the district vote in the presidential election against Trump. Case has positioned his seniority and tenure on the powerful House Appropriations Committee as critical assets for Hawaii, pointing to his role in securing federal resources for pandemic recovery, the Red Hill water crisis, and the aftermath of the Maui wildfires. “You can argue it all you want, but in Congress seniority matters,” Case told Hawaii Public Radio in July. Keohokalole has run on a platform of generational renewal, calling for more aggressive action on affordability, healthcare, and national policy issues. He has criticized Case for votes that alienated progressives, including his support for President Donald Trump's Safeguard American Voter Eligibility (SAVE) Act, and argued that the current political landscape demands a younger, more confrontational approach. Case told Hawaii Public Radio that the version of the SAVE Act he voted for provided accommodations for voters who don't present the required documentation, including signing a written attestation of their citizenship. He has voted against subsequent versions of the bill that didn't provide those accommodations. Case and Keohokalole were evenly matched in terms of campaign fundraising and spending, although Case had a sizable advantage in terms of cash in the bank heading into the campaign's final stretch. Why Democrats Are Watching The primary is the latest in a series of contests this cycle featuring progressive challengers targeting long-serving House Democrats, fueling broader debates over the party's future leadership and direction. While Case maintains advantages in name recognition and campaign funding, an upset by Keohokalole would signal continued appetite among Democratic voters to replace veteran lawmakers with younger alternatives. What Happens Next The winner will face Republican Adriel Lam, who is unopposed in the primary, in November's general election. Hawaii conducts its elections primarily by mail. Ballots are mailed to all registered voters. Less than 2 percent of 2024 state primary voters cast their ballots in person. As of Tuesday, about 179,000 ballots had already been cast in Saturday's election. Polls close at 7 p.m. local time, which is 1 a.m. ET Sunday. Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Steve Mollman and Anthony Murray.
news.summary: The outcome could offer another data point in the broader struggle between the party establishment and its progressive wing.

news.title: Joe Biden Health Update: Hunter Biden Says Former US President’s Cancer Has Spread and Is Causing Pain
news.text:
Former US President Joe Biden’s prostate cancer has spread to his bones and is causing him pain, his son Hunter Biden said in an interview with the BBC broadcast late Friday, August 7. Hunter Biden described his father’s condition as difficult for the family to watch, while saying the former president continues to remain engaged in public life.

Joe Biden, 83, revealed his cancer diagnosis in May 2025, less than four months after leaving the White House. His age and health had been major issues during his presidency, with questions about his condition intensifying after he ended his re-election campaign following a poor debate performance against Donald Trump.

Hunter Biden Says Joe Biden’s Cancer Has Spread

“I wish he would complain more, because it’s not good - the cancer has spread”
Hunter Biden discusses the health of his father, former US President Joe Biden. #Newsnight pic.twitter.com/QwNYjfithd
— BBC Newsnight (@BBCNewsnight) August 7, 2026

Hunter Biden Describes Father’s Condition

In the wide-ranging interview, Hunter Biden became emotional while discussing his father’s health. "The cancer has spread, metastasized into his bones and further," he said. "It's very painful and it's very debilitating in many respects."

Hunter Biden also spoke about the impact of the illness on the family. "It's really sad to watch. The only thing that I'd say about my dad, about his health right now, is I wish he would complain more, because it's not good." The comments provide a personal account of the former president’s condition, although details about his current medical treatment were not provided in the supplied interview.

Joe Biden Remains Active In Public Life

Despite his health problems, Hunter Biden said his father remains active and continues to speak publicly about issues that matter to him. "He's still doing his thing," he said. "He so believes in this country." Hunter Biden also said Joe Biden plans to publish a memoir titled Promise Me, America, after the mid-term elections.

Joe Biden disclosed his prostate cancer diagnosis in May 2025, shortly after leaving office. His office said at the time that the cancer was characterized by a Gleason score of 9, indicating an aggressive form of the disease, and that it had spread to his bones.

The former president subsequently began treatment for the disease. The latest comments from Hunter Biden indicate that the illness remains a significant health challenge for the former president.

Biden’s age was a recurring issue during his presidency. He became the oldest person to serve as US president and faced increasing scrutiny over his physical and mental fitness. news.title: Republicans tried to cut him off — then he beat them from the right
news.text:
This story was originally published by CalMatters. Sign up for their newsletters.

In the final weeks before the June primary, California GOP leaders took an unusual step. They sent a cease-and-desist letter to a sitting assemblymember accusing him of purposefully deceiving voters for his own benefit.

Officials alleged that San Diego lawmaker Carl DeMaio co-opted the official California Republican Party branding for his group Reform California’s campaign materials, calling them “a calculated deception of California’s Republican voters.”

It didn’t matter.

On Election Day, candidates backed by DeMaio’s Reform California performed well without the party’s endorsement, a sign of the growing influence of the renegade movement to the right of the California party.

Several of his candidates beat establishment Republican picks in the San Diego area, including in a closely watched state Senate race in which big tech and business groups spent $2 million to defeat Reform candidate Kristie Bruce-Lane. Despite that, Bruce-Lane beat out San Marcos City Councilmember Ed Musgrove and will face former Democratic San Diego City Attorney Mara Elliott in November.

As California Republicans brace for a challenging midterm election, they must navigate a reality in which DeMaio’s rabble-rousing politics prevail over pragmatic conservatism.

Reform also scored a win in the Central Valley, where Merced City Councilmember Darin DuPont advanced to compete against Democratic Assemblymember Esmeralda Soria.

The group even prevailed in local races, including a San Diego County supervisor race, in which Reform-backed San Marcos Mayor Rebecca Jones secured 38% of the vote, besting Vista Mayor John Franklin, the establishment pick.

Republican gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton also has a friend in DeMaio, according to Hilton spokesperson Hector Barajas. Hilton appeared on DeMaio’s daily podcast in the run-up to the June primary.

“Steve is proud to have the support of Reform California and values his relationship with Carl DeMaio,” Barajas said in a statement. DeMaio’s group had endorsed both Hilton and Riverside County Sheriff Chad Bianco in the primary.

DeMaio declined multiple interview requests from CalMatters for this story in person and did not respond to phone, email and text messages. 

San Diego Senate race

Bruce-Lane’s candidacy in Senate District 40 was a top concern for local Republicans. After she lost two previous legislative races, some worried she wouldn’t be their best shot at holding the seat currently held by Senate Minority Leader Brian Jones, who terms out this year.

This dispute was at the center of an explosive February meeting when San Diego GOP committee members couldn’t agree on whether to back Bruce-Lane or Musgrove, who was endorsed by established Republicans including Jones and outgoing U.S. Rep. Darrell Issa.

The two are similar on policy, but not on temperament. DeMaio and others call Bruce-Lane a “fighter” who will tussle with Democrats on the chamber floor, something DeMaio is known for in the Democratic-controlled Legislature, where his caucus is outnumbered three-to-one.

Musgrove and those who backed him represent the party’s more diplomatic old guard who cut deals with Democrats behind the scenes to advance their legislative priorities.

Musgrove received $1.3 million in support from super PAC California Leads, a joint Meta-Google venture to boost candidates who oppose strict tech regulations, and nearly $530,000 from a super PAC funded by Chevron and other oil companies, according to campaign finance records.

Bruce-Lane raised about $250,000 and received $2,000 in independent expenditures from DeMaio’s Reform Local Government PAC and nearly $13,000 from the San Diego County Gun Owners PAC.

Reform corrected the fliers and website misusing the official party branding, said California Republican Party Chair Corrin Rankin, who has a poor relationship with DeMaio. 

DeMaio and the candidates he backs are fighters who are willing to be agitators, Republican political strategist Jon Fleischman said. Republicans’ pragmatism in the statehouse largely comes down to the kind of people supported and elected by the official party infrastructure, he said. 

DeMaio frequently votes against bills, an anomaly in the California Legislature where most lawmakers — Democrats and Republicans — choose not to vote at all to maintain relationships and donors.

“Carl will always err toward finding somebody who’s willing to actually make noise in Sacramento,” he said. “Carl’s argument is: We don’t have the votes, all we have is our voice.”

A longtime local official with a low-key demeanor, Musgrove likely wasn’t going to be that.

“What a nice guy, I met him a few times, and I thought, you know, ‘He’s a very pleasant fellow. I wouldn’t mind having dinner or lunch with this guy,” Fleischman said. “But is this guy going to be a bomb thrower on the floor of the state Assembly? He’s gonna be more of a gentleman.”

Musgrove said it’s possible Bruce-Lane beat him because of her outspokenness, but being pragmatic is how bills get passed.

“I have to believe she has a strategy to go up there and effectuate change rather than continuing to point out problems,” he said.

To moderate or activate the base?

As Democrats outnumber Republicans 45% to 25% in voter registration and haven’t won a statewide race in California for 20 years, a longstanding question remains at the forefront for the state party: whether to moderate its positions to broaden the membership or lean right to rile up support among the base.

Reform California’s aggressive approach poses one potential answer, with its ability to raise millions of dollars from small-dollar donors, bringing in a total of $5.8 million during the 2024 campaign cycle, about a quarter of what the entire state Republican Party raised in the same period. 

Reform California also successfully put a voter ID initiative, Proposition 39, on the November ballot and it’s bringing life — and hopefully voters — back into the party, strategists say.

“DeMaio has built a very formidable and good political organization,” even though some people may not like it, GOP consultant Tim Rosales said. “California state politics is big league baseball. You got to have thick skin and you gotta be able to roll with it.”

But Republicans are expected to face an uphill battle in the San Diego Senate race and elsewhere come November.

“This is a seat that’s going to be very difficult for Republicans to retain in a midterm election, so it’s not surprising that the leadership was preferring a more mainstream candidate,” Republican strategist Rob Stutzman said.

“The primary base in each party often does not pick the most competitive candidate in a swing seat in a general election. But it also doesn’t mean it should be written off.”

Bruce-Lane did not return multiple calls from CalMatters seeking an interview.

A sought-after target for Democrats, the inland San Diego district leans Republican but has trended increasingly purple in recent years. Former Vice President Kamala Harris won it by nearly 4 percentage points and nearly 35% of registered voters there are Democrats, while 34% are Republicans and 24% have no party preference.

Rankin, the state GOP chair, wouldn’t say whether she’s concerned about the party’s ability to retain Jones’ seat with Bruce-Lane as the candidate. 

“The only thing I’m saying from my position is that we have a Republican who made it past the primary. I think it’s going to be up to the voters,” she said.

An old playbook

DeMaio’s strategy reflects a longstanding feud over the party’s direction that has caused problems for Republican Party chairs throughout the last several decades, as agitators within the party tried to push it rightward, consultant Rosales said. 

Former George W. Bush administrator Gerry Parksy attempted to remake the California Republican Party from the inside out in 2001 by restructuring its budget committee and pushing for moderate platforms in an effort to appeal to women and nonwhite voters. It wreaked havoc as party officials feared moderating would forgo traditional viewpoints on sex, marriage and immigration.

“What’s the point of a minority party if you’re not expressing the minority view?”Republican political strategist Jon Fleischman

Then-Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger, the last Republican to hold statewide office, famously implored the state party to broaden its tent, telling delegates in 2007 that the party was “dying at the box office” and alienating women and nonwhite voters by ignoring things like the environment and healthcare. Party officials largely ignored his pleas. 

Other rifts have appeared under Rankin’s leadership since she took over last year. 

Some questioned her fundraising ability. In response, Jones and other party leaders announced a change in how campaign donations from their committees are distributed to the party, further weakening its electoral power.

Some welcome the divisiveness.

“I happen to be on the side of more voices like Carl would be better, because I don’t think there should be a free pass on the floor of the Legislature,” Fleischman said. “What’s the point of a minority party if you’re not expressing the minority view?”

news.title: Kamala Harris Lost, So Naturally the Electoral College Is Broken
news.text:
Kamala Harris is back on the road, and apparently the 2024 election taught her one lesson above all others: the system must be the problem.

During a Friday swing through New Orleans, the former vice president told students she plans to spend the next several months rallying voters across the South. Harris tied the tour to the Supreme Court’s decision in Louisiana v. Callais, which she claimed, “basically undid the Voting Rights Act.” She also accused Republicans of trying to cheat ahead of the November midterms.

“I’m spending my time to remind people that even though they’re trying to put obstacles in front of us, even though they’re trying to cheat — because they are trying to cheat,” Harris said, “that that’s not a reason that we just stay in bed and keep the covers over our heads and say, ‘well, wake me up when it’s over.’”

Stirring stuff. A sober defense of democracy from the woman currently crisscrossing the country to tell Democrats that the other side cheats, the Electoral College is rigged, and what her party really needs is more "ruthlessness." At the same rally, Harris was welcomed as "Madame President." The Electoral College apparently missed that memo.

Harris spent Friday barnstorming New Orleans. She addressed hundreds of students at an InspireNOLA back-to-school rally in the morning, then headlined the Louisiana Democrat Party’s “Masquerade Sneaker Ball” that evening. New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno also presented her with a ceremonial key to the city at a private event before the gala. Apparently losing the presidency comes with perks.

Read More: Kamala Peddles Election Rigging Conspiracies While Ignoring 270,000 Illegal Voters

Prepared excerpts supplied ahead of Harris’s evening address said Democrats needed to develop a “ruthlessness that must be the attitude of the Democratic Party.” She was careful to explain that she meant the nice kind of ruthlessness.

“This fight requires that we start to get comfortable with some things — including having a certain kind of ruthlessness. Now, I don’t mean ruthlessness like the cruelty they show. I mean the kind that is uncompromising in its impatience with injustice, that shows no mercy for corruption, that fights back hard when they threaten the power of the people.”

Compassionate ruthlessness. Ruthlessness with guardrails. Ruthlessness that went through a focus group and came back approved for a Democratic fundraiser.

The prepared remarks were less delicate when Harris described the Republican Party. She called it morally corrupt and accused it of wanting to “sow chaos, grab wealth and abuse power.”

“The good news is Donald Trump will be term limited out. However, please let us be clear: there is no term limit on this new Republican Party built in his image — and folks, there is a deep moral corruption about this new Republican Party. Their ideology is clearly to create a smash-and-grab world. To sow chaos, grab wealth and abuse power.”

Republicans cheat. Republicans are morally corrupt. Democrats need to show no mercy. The coconut tree and the brat summer are over. This is the ruthlessness era.

The New Orleans appearance followed another Harris speech on July 31 at the National Urban League Conference in Nashville. There, while laying out ideas for Democrats ahead of the midterms and the 2028 presidential race, she floated reopening one of her party’s favorite grievances.

“I know this is going to be controversial coming from me in particular — we need to revisit the Electoral College.”

Harris didn't say what "revisit" actually means. The timing is its own punchline. Trump beat her in the Electoral College in 2024, and won the popular vote. There is no machinery to blame. There is only the outcome.

The welcome was not unanimous. Outside the gala, protesters hit Harris over her support for Israel and demanded the DNC finally release its autopsy of the 2024 loss, the one party leadership has been sitting on. Her own coalition is already relitigating why she lost before she has even announced she is running again.

Harris is reportedly considering another presidential run in 2028. Her early message now includes cheating Republicans, a morally corrupt opposition party, Democratic ruthlessness, and fresh questions about the Electoral College. For a politician who secured the 2024 nomination after Joe Biden quit the race, without winning a presidential primary of her own, the democracy lecture could still use some work.

news.title: Trump pulls stunning election fraud claim out of his pocket in new interview: ‘They rigged him out of it’
news.text:
President Donald Trump is claiming another election was “rigged” against a Republican candidate, this time pointing to former Rep. Mike Rogers’ narrow loss in the 2024 Michigan Senate race.

Trump made the claim during a new interview with Jake Sherman of Punchbowl News while discussing the Republican Party’s prospects heading into the 2026 midterm elections. 

When Sherman said that Rogers lost his 2024 Senate bid while Trump was also on the ballot in Michigan, Trump said, “But I happen to think he won.”

“Ok, well–” Sherman interjected.

“No, no. I think it was a rigged deal,” Trump interrupted. “I think they rigged him out of it. 

“But he’s a very good candidate,” Trump said in the interviewed published late Friday. “I think he should do well if we believe in polls. I actually sort of believe in polls.”

The Independent has contacted Rogers’ representative for comment. 

Rogers, a former Michigan congressman, narrowly lost the 2024 Senate race to Democrat Elissa Slotkin. Slotkin received about 2.71 million votes, compared with nearly 2.69 million for Rogers, giving her a victory margin of less than 20,000 votes. The results were certified, and a subsequent standard audit did not uncover evidence that the election had been stolen. 

Trump’s claim comes despite his own victory in Michigan in 2024, where he defeated then-Vice President Kamala Harris by about 1.4 percentage points while Rogers lost to Slotkin by about 0.3 points. Trump also made a similar claim in January, saying the Senate race had been rigged against Rogers.

“I’ll be honest with you, Mike. They rigged the election on you. Mine was too big to rig. You won, I’m telling you, you won, but you’re going to do great this time,” 

Rogers is getting another chance in 2026. He won the Republican nomination this week and will face Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in November for Michigan's open Senate seat. The contest is expected to be closely watched as Republicans and Democrats battle for control of the Senate. 

During Friday’s interview, Trump also discussed El-Sayed, referring to the Democrat by what the president claimed was his real name.

“It’s ‘Abdul,’ but I call him ‘Abdullah,'” Trump said. “The actual name is ‘Abdullah,’ and then it’s much longer than that. But if you believe in the polls, [Rogers] does better against Abdullah than he did against the young congresswoman [Haley Stevens].”

El-Sayed’s full name is Abdulrahman Mohamed El-Sayed. He has previously accused Rogers and other political opponents of using his full name as a racist dog whistle.

“They think they want to use my whole name against me,” El-Sayed told supporters Wednesday, the day after he won the primary. “Mike, listen, man, if you can’t say the name, it’s Abdulrahman, keep the name out of your d**n mouth. I’ll be happy to give you lessons.”
news.summary: Trump won Michigan on the same ballot he now says was ‘rigged’

news.title: Joe Biden’s son: ‘Dad’s cancer has spread to his bones and beyond’
news.text: Former U.S. President Joe Biden’s prostate cancer has spread to other parts of his body and is causing significant pain, his son Hunter Biden said in an emotional interview with the BBC. Hunter Biden grew tearful as he discussed his 83-year-old father’s worsening condition. “The cancer has spread, metastasized into his bones and further,” he said. “It’s very painful and it's very debilitating in many respects.” “It’s really sad to watch,” Biden added. “The only thing that I'd say about my dad, about his health right now, is I wish he would complain more, because it’s not good.” Despite his illness, Hunter said the former president remains engaged with public life and continues speaking about issues important to him. “He’s still doing his thing,” Hunter said. “He so believes in this country.” Joe Biden was diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer in May 2025, less than four months after leaving the White House. He subsequently began treatment that included radiation and hormone therapy. Hunter said the diagnosis had been difficult for the entire family, describing his father as its continuing center. He also revisited the June 2024 presidential debate against Donald Trump, a performance that intensified concerns about Biden’s age and fitness for office and ultimately contributed to his withdrawal from the presidential race. “I was shocked. I knew something was wrong,” Hunter said. He attributed his father’s poor performance in part to physical exhaustion caused by extensive travel while serving as president. Hunter also questioned whether the cancer diagnosed the following year might already have been affecting his father at the time. Joe Biden eventually ended his reelection campaign and endorsed then-Vice President Kamala Harris as the Democratic nominee. Hunter also addressed the sweeping presidential pardon his father granted him shortly before leaving office. He acknowledged that the decision was “unfair” to the American public, while defending his father’s personal choice. “What would you think about my dad if he didn't do it for me?” he asked. Joe Biden pardoned his son in two federal cases less than two months before leaving the White House. Hunter Biden had been convicted of federal gun charges after prosecutors said he purchased and possessed a firearm while using drugs and falsely stated on a federal form that he was not an unlawful drug user. He had also pleaded guilty to federal tax charges in California. The pardon was issued before sentencing in either case. During the BBC interview, Hunter also spoke candidly about the depths of his addiction, saying that at one stage he was drinking nearly four liters of vodka a day and smoking crack cocaine approximately every 15 minutes. “It was hell on Earth,” he said. Hunter ruled out following his father into politics, saying he instead wants to devote his time to helping others struggling with addiction. Joe Biden, meanwhile, is expected to publish a memoir titled “Promise Me, America” after the midterm elections.
news.summary: Former president’s son tells BBC the disease is ‘very painful’ and debilitating, recalls being shocked by Biden’s 2024 debate performance and discusses the presidential pardon he received before his father left office
