news.title: Trump is blocking billions of dollars of grants that would fix the grid
news.text:
In Wisconsin, utility Alliant Energy has called off a project meant to reduce power outages in disadvantaged and tribal communities, after the Trump administration terminated a federal grant that would have supported it.

In California, the Sacramento Municipal Utility District, which has deployed and upgraded hundreds of thousands of advanced smart meters, has not received any reimbursement from the U.S. Department of Energy, or DOE, for the work since October, when the Trump administration declared it was killing grants that it described as fueling ​“the Left’s climate agenda.”

And in the upper Midwest, a consortium of regional grid operators, utilities, and state agencies is still waiting for $464 million in DOE funds meant to help build high-voltage transmission lines to reduce grid congestion — although the agency in charge of the project says the funding will soon be restored.

Across the country, hundreds of such projects to improve grid reliability and make electricity more affordable face a highly uncertain future — the result of Trump administration actions that have slowed the outflow of billions of dollars of DOE funds to a trickle.

Some of those projects in ​“blue states” were targeted as political retribution, as recent reporting from The New York Times has made clear. A handful of grant awardees in this category have won favorable court rulings, and more are seeking legal redress.

But many others are suffering from the DOE’s broader failure to carry out work that Congress has tasked it to do, according to groups that have been monitoring the agency since the start of last year. In red and blue states alike, the DOE is forcing thousands of grantees to undergo a laborious review process, so even projects that have not been officially terminated are stuck, unable to determine when or if they’ll start getting the money they’re owed.

According to an April report from the DOE Alumni Network, a group of former agency employees, the DOE has announced the termination of 356 awards totaling $12.5 billion since January 2025, and has threatened to terminate 303 additional awards worth $12.2 billion.

But the DOE has also stalled projects for ​“a large number of awardees who have never appeared on any list,” the report found. ​“This means the agency is not moving forward to resolve disputes, finalize conditional awards, or respond to continuation applications, leaving projects in administrative limbo and functionally freezing promised funds.”

“DOE both overtly canceled a set of projects, then had this pattern of behavior where for 15 months they stopped actively managing projects,” said one former DOE official. ​“Projects can’t proceed to the next stages and get their next tranche of funding.”

The former official, who asked not to be named, described a pattern of stalling, stonewalling, and ​“ghosting” utilities, state governments, energy companies, and nonprofit groups awarded grants under the Biden administration.

Many of those projects have been caught up in a process the DOE announced in May 2025 to review all financial assistance ​“on a case-by-case basis to identity [sic] waste of taxpayer dollars, protect America’s national security and advance President Trump’s commitment to unleash affordable, reliable and secure energy for the American people.”

Then, in October, the DOE announced the ​“termination of 321 financial awards supporting 223 projects” — all of them tied to states that voted for Kamala Harris in the 2024 election. The DOE’s termination announcement came right after Russ Vought, director of the White House Office of Management and Budget, declared in a social media post that the administration would cancel ​“nearly $8 billion in Green New Scam funding.”

Canary Media reached out to a subset of DOE grantees that had won funding from the Grid Resilience and Innovation Partnerships (GRIP) program created by the 2021 bipartisan infrastructure law. The DOE issued a total of more than 100 GRIP grants — in October 2023, August 2024, and October 2024 — for projects to enlarge the grid, harden it against extreme weather, build microgrids to protect vulnerable communities, and deploy technologies to integrate solar, wind, EVs, and batteries.

Some of the GRIP projects involve expanding clean energy and serving disadvantaged communities, two bugbears of the Trump administration. But many more are straightforward grid improvement projects that need federal dollars to reduce the costs borne by utilities and regional or state agencies.

The largest of these is in California. In 2024, the DOE awarded a $630.6 million grant aimed at upgrading more than 100 miles of high-voltage power lines in the state with advanced power cables capable of carrying more electricity along existing transmission corridors, a project estimated to be capable of delivering about $200 million in savings from improved energy efficiency. That project was terminated in October, and the DOE has disbursed no money for it, according to federal records.

This uncertainty appears to apply to the majority of GRIP projects, according to Emlyn Bottomley, founder of the consultancy High Road Analytics, which focuses on workforce development, and a former Department of Labor deputy policy director in the Biden administration.

According to his tracking of federal spending, of the roughly $11.4 billion in DOE funds obligated to grid infrastructure and resilience — a category that includes GRIP program funds — $9.1 billion remains ​“at risk,” with funding stalled or timelines for completion shortened. That’s compared with $400 million in grants that have been canceled outright and $1.3 billion not yet disbursed but showing no signs of being stalled.

“It’s a shame these projects are being held up or canceled, especially since the case for them is fairly bipartisan — spanning national security, economic competitiveness, and cost and affordability,” Bottomley said.

All of the GRIP projects required partners to provide matching funds at an amount at least equal to the money DOE is providing, the former DOE official added. ​“You’re talking about folks putting hundreds of millions of dollars on the line. People have skin in the game for these awards.”

The costs of losing federal funding

Many of the GRIP grantees contacted by Canary Media declined to comment, citing ongoing discussions with DOE. Others reported that they are no longer pursuing the projects as described in their grant applications, at least not with the help of DOE money.

The latter is the case for Alliant Energy’s Smart Power Automation in Rural Communities (SPARC) project, which won a $50 million grant in late 2024 to add grid visibility and control devices to 140 grid circuits in disadvantaged and tribal communities served by subsidiary Wisconsin Power & Light — a utility in a blue state.

Those devices could allow the utility to quickly find and isolate faults on its grid, cutting power outages in targeted communities by up to 50 percent. They could also support grid-management software to help integrate more renewable and distributed energy, and potentially expand wireless communications access to these remote areas.

Alliant ​“voluntarily withdrew” from the grant award process in April, six months after its grant was terminated by the DOE, Alliant spokesperson Melissa McCarville told Canary Media. The agency has disbursed no funds to the project, according to federal records.

Alliant is ​“actively pursuing many of the goals that were outlined in the SPARC project,” McCarville wrote in a May email, but as part of a 10-year strategic plan with no set timeline. ​“While the grant did provide valuable funding, it also required a significant investment, and we want to ensure our contributions are properly prioritized,” she wrote.

Still, at least one grant-funded project in a blue state is proceeding despite the absence of DOE funds. 

That’s the case for the Sacramento Municipal Utility District, which serves the state’s capitol and environs. In 2023, SMUD won a $50 million grant to support a project to deploy 200,000 smart meters and grid devices and underlying software controls to ​“improve grid reliability, resilience, visibility and efficiency,” utility spokesperson Gamaliel Ortiz told Canary Media in an email. 

SMUD has carried out much of that work, which includes close to $100 million in utility spending, and has received almost $33 million in reimbursements from DOE, according to federal records. However, SMUD ​“has not received reimbursement for any costs incurred after the grant was cancelled on October 10, 2025,” Ortiz wrote. ​“We remain committed to this critical work and stay flexible as we evaluate how the loss of grant funding may impact the project timeline.”

In other blue states, some grants have been canceled and others are still under negotiation. In Oregon, utility Portland General Electric has recently learned that the DOE may reinstate a previously terminated $50 million grant to support next-generation ​“grid edge computing” devices, utility spokesperson John Farmer told Canary Media in an August email. That project had received only $1.2 million in DOE funding, according to federal records.

The purpose of the project was to integrate batteries, EVs, and community solar into its grid to ​“improve resilience, enable the integration of distributed energy resources, and maximize customer investments in home energy solutions.”

“PGE is evaluating the benefits and risks of reinstating the grant,” Farmer told Canary Media. The utility ​“recognizes that there are inherent risks of additional and changing demands by the DOE as the administration’s priorities change.”

At the same time, PGE remains in discussion with the DOE on a $250 million grant to build a high-voltage transmission line with the Confederated Tribes of Warm Springs, Farmer wrote. ​“Without this funding, we would lose the opportunity to offset those costs with external dollars, which could limit how efficiently we can advance needed grid improvements.”

Red state projects are also being held up because the grantee is located in a blue state. Such is the case of the aforementioned $464 million DOE grant for the Joint Targeted Interconnection Queue project to build new transmission lines between the Midcontinent Independent System Operator and Southwest Power Pool, two grid operators spanning nearly a dozen Midwestern states.

The $464 million GRIP grant was meant to bolster $1.3 billion in matching funds from utilities in the region to enable nearly 30 gigawatts of new generation to be built in Iowa, Kansas, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, North Dakota, and South Dakota. All but one of those states voted for Donald Trump in the 2024 election — but the Minnesota Department of Commerce, the entity awarded the grant, is in a blue state.

In May, the Minnesota Department of Commerce announced that the DOE ​“will honor its $464 million grant,” which will ​“unlock more than $1 billion in additional private investment and provide communities across the region with economic and infrastructure benefits.”

A DOE spokesperson told Canary Media in a July email that the DOE has conducted its review of GRIP projects based on a ​“number of criteria,” including whether it has ​“achieved the milestones set forth in the terms of the award,” whether it ​“remains technically and economically feasible,” and whether it ​“continues to effectuate the purpose of the program or the Department’s priorities.”

The spokesperson added that ​“none of the termination decisions were based on political considerations.” That statement is belied by court testimony reported by The New York Times last month, in which a DOE lawyer stated that none of the October grant terminations were ​“based on any programmatic, statutory, cost-reduction or performance-based factor,” and that all but one of them ​“had a recipient location and/​or at least one place of performance in a state that awarded its electoral votes to Kamala Harris in the 2024 election and has two Democratic-caucusing senators.”

During a series of congressional hearings in April, Energy Secretary Chris Wright stated that the DOE’s review of more than 20,000 grants was almost complete, and that more than 80 percent of grantees had received notice that their awards could proceed as is or with modifications.

But an Alumni Network analysis of DOE data shared with Congress showed that the DOE’s review both failed to restore the vast majority of projects caught up in the ​“blue state” termination action in October and failed to address the hundreds of projects that have never been officially terminated but remain unable to secure funds.

The revelation of the DOE’s explicit targeting of blue states for grant termination spurred 39 Senate Democrats to sign a letter to Wright and Vought demanding the immediate restoration of funding for DOE projects terminated in October.

“Once an administration begins punishing Americans for how they vote,” the senators wrote, ​“the threat extends far beyond these projects: no state, community, business, or worker can trust that the federal government will apply the law fairly.”
news.summary: The Department of Energy has canceled or stalled funding for thousands of projects that would improve the country’s stressed grid — and not just in blue states.

news.title: Former U.S. President Joe Biden’s Cancer Spreads, Son Reveals

He told supporters last month that therapy was “going really well” and thanked them for their prayers and encouragement.Despite his health challenges, Hunter emphasized his father’s central role in the family: “My dad is, to this day, the centre of our family. He’s the best father, the best husband, the best grandfather.”

Biden stepped away from the 2024 presidential race, paving the way for Vice President Kamala Harris to become the Democratic nominee. 

His memoir, Promise Me, America, is scheduled for release in November.

news.title: Joe Biden’s cancer has spread to bones, son reveals
news.text:
Former United States President Joe Biden’s prostate cancer has spread to his bones, with his son, Hunter Biden, revealing that the former president is now battling a painful and debilitating stage of the disease.

Hunter made the disclosure in an interview with the BBC published on Saturday while speaking about his father’s ongoing treatment.

He said Biden’s condition had become increasingly difficult for the family to watch, describing the illness as painful and debilitating.

“I wish he would complain more, because it’s not good, the cancer has spread,” Hunter said.

According to him, the cancer has metastasised to Biden’s bones and spread further.

“It’s very painful… very debilitating. Cancer is really hard. It’s really sad to watch,” he added.

Hunter, Biden’s only surviving son, also described the former president as the centre of their family.

“My dad is, to this day, the centre of our family. He’s the best father, the best husband, the best grandfather,” he said.

Biden announced in May 2025, months after leaving office, that he had been diagnosed with an aggressive form of prostate cancer.

At the time, the former president said doctors expected him to respond to treatment and described his prognosis as good.

“The prognosis is good, we’re working on it,” Biden had said.

He also thanked those who offered prayers and support during his treatment.

Biden’s health had been a major subject of public discussion during the final months of his presidency and his 2024 presidential campaign.

He withdrew from the 2024 presidential race in July 2024 and was subsequently replaced as the Democratic presidential nominee by then-Vice President Kamala Harris, who lost the election to Donald Trump.

Biden has since spent more time with his family while undergoing treatment.

news.title: Anxious students who were unenrolled now moving into Howard University dorms
news.text:
WASHINGTON (AP) — Nikiyah Clark had five boxes and a backpack when she ultimately received the keys to her Howard University dorm. Weeks earlier, the school had told her this moment would never come.

When Howard administrators informed Clark — and hundreds of others — that she was permanently unenrolled for missing a tuition fee deadline, she rode a bus from Cleveland, Ohio, to plea with administrators. She left in tears.

“I didn’t just lose my dream. I lost my way out,” said the 17-year-old, who had pinned her hopes on Howard as a peaceful environment and a path to financial freedom after years of growing up in “survival mode.”

Shortly after that, the university notified Clark she was once again welcome to enroll. But as she moved into the Washington, D.C., campus on Thursday, she remained uneasy. She worries that the university might reverse its decision yet again, and hopes Howard will make changes so that other students aren’t wrongfully unenrolled.

“I’m definitely not really over that,” Clark said.

While administrators prefer that students, faculty and alumni focus on the school’s new academic year, much of the community’s attention is still trained on the unenrollment debacle. More than 500 incoming first-year students were unenrolled for missing a July tuition payment deadline, the university said. About 200 students have had their enrollment restored.

It was also reported Friday that Howard unenrolled the students about a month after offering voluntary early retirement buyouts to 600 eligible employees. But Howard University said in a statement that the employee buyouts were unrelated and part of a plan for “long-term financial sustainability.”

For some in the Howard community, the bitter experience has raised questions about the legacy of one of the country’s most revered historically Black colleges and universities. Others say such administrative matters won’t lessen the career impact a Howard diploma can have.

The loss of HBCU luster

Zy’Aira Blackmon had her heart set on attending Howard, seen as the preeminent Black university in the nation.

But, after her enrollment status was revoked and then reinstated within days, the 18-year-old from Grand Rapids, Michigan, doesn’t feel the same way. The luster Howard once held has been dulled.

“After this situation, most people are going to ignore all the good things Howard has to offer,” said Blackmon, who now will study at Western Michigan University.

When Howard took away 17-year-old Yuisa Davis’ enrollment, her mother hopped on a plane July 28 from the family’s Puerto Rico home to get answers. An administrative official told Karina Polen-Davis and her husband, who was on speakerphone, that she couldn’t answer their questions. Then the official called security.

The Davises say they paid what they thought they owed but the university rescinded enrollment without explanation or recourse.

The school never budged.

“It’s very disheartening just because there’s so many opportunities that’s kind of just been taken from me without me being able to” find a resolution, said Yuisa Davis, who often visited Howard as a child.

Now, Davis is working with The New School in New York City on possible financial aid.

“The difference in how we’ve been treated has been night and day,” Kenneth Davis said.

Families and university officials blame miscommunication

Interim President Wayne A. I. Frederick told The Associated Press last month that Howard simply followed its payment policy, noting that 2,200 students did meet payment requirements.

Unenrolled students and their parents did not properly read school communications about a July 10 deadline for half their unpaid balance, with financial aid factored in, Frederick said.

Those students who did everything correctly “deserve to show up on Aug. 17, the first day of class and meet their professors in class, have their housing assignments taken care of,” Frederick said. Previously, the school had to scramble to find enough student housing and adjunct professors to fill classrooms.

Some students assert they followed the school’s payment requirements.

Blackmon said her scholarship had not been included in her balance owed. After being unenrolled, she constantly called and emailed the school.

“They reinstated me. They really didn’t explain much,” she added.

Ashley Christopher, an attorney and Howard alumna whose son is a sophomore there, thinks Howard shoulders some blame. She is the founder of HBCU Week, a foundation that awards scholarships, and believes students received “bad information” from the school.

“There’s a way to take accountability for a misstep, and also explain that there’s joint responsibility here,” said Christopher, an attorney. “It is not just the parents. It’s not just the students.”

Frederick said that how Howard has handled unenrollment and reenrollment can contribute positively to the school’s image.

“All this does is strengthen our legacy and helps us perform as a high-performing institution on the administrative side, as we have been doing in the past,” he said.

A storied and pree

minent HBCU

The nearly 160-year-old Howard is one of about 100 HBCUs in the U.S., with famous alumni including former Vice President Kamala Harris and actor Chadwick Boseman.

Howard has a 6-year graduation rate of 70% and a retention rate of 90%, according to the U.S. Department of Education’s Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System. The school consistently ranks among the most prestigious private HBCUs, including as the top-ranked HBCU by Forbes.

The university costs more than $66,000 each year to attend. The median income for four-year graduates is about $73,000, according to the Education Department. Frederick said Howard has graduated more Black doctors than any other school in the country.

The “scandal,” as Christopher calls the unenrollment issue, likely will not impact Howard’s reputation as “The Mecca” of Black education in the long run.

“Howard has been the blueprint for HBCUs, graduated the best and the brightest — not saying they’re the only one who does that,” she said. “When it comes to overall impact of HBCU institutions, Howard stands at the top of that list.”

___ Tang reported from Sunnyvale, California. Williams reported from Detroit.

news.title: Colorado's socialist surge shakes up the Democratic establishment
news.text: Democratic socialist candidate Melat Kiros shocked Colorado’s Democratic establishment when she defeated 15-term incumbent Rep. Diana DeGette in the state's June primary. The double-digit win exposed a growing rift over the party's values that has left some Democrats stunned and questioning the future of the party. "If you had told me this woman would have won by 13 points, I would have bet my house against that," Doug Friednash, a veteran political strategist in Colorado, told Fox News Digital. "I never would have thought we would have seen a victory of that magnitude here in Denver." Friednash has tracked Colorado's political shift from red to deep blue over the past three decades, previously serving in the state legislature representing House District 10 in Denver. He later served as Denver city attorney and chief of staff to former Colorado Gov. John Hickenlooper, and he currently works as a partner at Brownstein, a prominent legal and lobbying firm in the region. Kiros' victory was one of dozens of wins for far-left candidates in Democratic primary elections this cycle as socialists continue to ascend across the country. The far-left's rise in the party has alarmed seasoned Democrats like Friednash. JEWISH COMMUNITY IN DENVER ON HIGH ALERT OVER RISE OF DEMOCRATIC SOCIALIST MELAT KIROS "It was one thing watching this happen in New York ... But when it happens in a state like Colorado, which is really the gateway to the West, it tells me that this issue is going to spread and may be a cancer to the Democratic Party if they don't figure out what our values are," Friednash said. He noted that Kiros' victory did not happen in a vacuum, pointing out that DSA-backed candidates have successfully captured seats in the state legislature and city councils over the past few years. While Friednash originally predicted Rep. Diana DeGette would win, he acknowledged Kiros' campaign had a strong ground game and was able to tap into anti-establishment sentiments among progressives in the region. Kiros' team reportedly knocked on more than 100,000 voters' doors and ran a phone bank reaching 500,000 people leading up to election night. SOCIALISM’S RISE INSIDE THE DEMOCRATIC PARTY NOW THREATENS THE AMERICAN DREAM She also campaigned on fighting for universal healthcare, affordable housing, utilities and more. Friednash said Kiros' message resonated with younger voters who are frustrated by the high cost of living and feel let down by the Democratic establishment. "I think the number one issue is affordability, by far," he said. "A lot of younger people that have moved to Denver have come here wanting to buy a house. They can't buy a home, it seems unaffordable and unattainable. And I think she's tapped into a lot of voter anger and hostility over things not being better." He believes Denver has become a microcosm of the national debate taking place within the Democratic Party over its future direction. Comparing the DSA wave to the rise of the MAGA movement within the Republican Party, Friednash warned that if party leadership refuses to call out the group's extreme policies, it will ultimately hurt Democrats in swing districts across the nation. RAHM EMANUEL WARNS DSA AGENDA DOESN'T PLAY WELL OUTSIDE 'UPPER WEST SIDE OF MANHATTAN' "As I look out at what's happening within the Democratic Party, you know, it's kind of like a ship without a captain," Friednash said. "A lot of the more mainstream Democrats, rather than trying to say, 'Here are the issues we should be fighting about,' are embracing the socialists, because I think they're afraid of them... much like I think we've seen with the MAGA movement." "While some Democrats may be falling in love with socialism, you know who isn't? The rest of America," he continued. "That dog's not gonna hunt in these more competitive primaries." Prominent centrist Democratic groups such as Third Way share that anxiety. The organization recently told The New York Times it plans to launch a $15 million campaign to combat the Democratic Socialists of America movement, which it believes poses a "mortal danger" to Democrats and will hurt the party in potential presidential swing states. Concerns over the party's ideological turn aren't limited to establishment Democrats. Jon Caldara, president of the Denver-based free-market think tank Independence Institute, also questions the future of his home state as democratic socialists continue to rise in prominence. "Without a doubt, the Democratic Party in Colorado has changed," Caldara told Fox News Digital, arguing the state has abandoned its historically pro-business stance. Caldara, a libertarian and longtime radio host and columnist, is outspoken about the challenges facing Denver and the broader state, such as affordability, homelessness and an exodus of businesses. He believes these issues will worsen, warning that establishment Democrats have lost control of their own party. "When the state started turning left, this machine was so powerful, it really couldn't stop itself," Caldara said. "And now it's really beginning to eat their own. It's kind of a French Revolution thing that you see that the Democratic Party here in Colorado is now well out over their skis. And there is a growing fight between Democrats and socialists." "The real telltale is that Democrats are afraid to speak the truth because they don't want to get canceled," he added. "It is vicious to go against the socialists." SHOCKING PERCENTAGE OF DEMOCRATS IDENTIFY AS 'DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS' ACCORDING TO NEW POLL: 'TOXIC POLICIES' Caldara believes younger voters are increasingly being drawn to democratic socialist candidates in Denver and across the country because they lack historical context for how these types of policies have fared across the world. "Sadly, the young suffer from a terrible disease: It's called youth. And because they're young, they haven't seen failed socialism around the globe," Caldara said. "They haven't seen what happened in the Soviet Union. They haven't learned the lesson of Sweden, which looked like such a wonderful socialist paradise until it didn't work, and now they're turning into a capitalist system. They haven't seen this." "So the idea that we can just redistribute rich guys' money sounds great," he continued. "We'll just do rent control. We'll do government funding. We all know how that's going to end up. It's going to end up poorly. And young people are going to be hurt." "I'm sad that they want to run this experiment again," he added. "And it's even sadder that it's happening in this beautiful free state, this western state, this pro-free-enterprise state of Colorado." Longtime Colorado residents like Gene Maine understand full well why socialist policies are appealing. But having fled the Soviet Union as a teenager in 1981, Maine sees unsettling parallels between the society he grew up in and the direction Denver is headed. As a child, Maine said he was often told that America, Western Europe and capitalism were evil. But as he got older, he realized the utopian society he was supposedly living in wasn't all that it was cracked up to be. REPUBLICANS SOUND ALARM OVER FAR-LEFT GROUP'S PUSH TO TRANSFORM AMERICA INTO 'CUBAN DICTATORSHIP' "As I grew older, I started recognizing that, ‘Oh my God, I'm being lied to. We're all being lied to," Maine recalled. "This is not the freest society in the world. It's a jail." After defecting from the USSR with his mother as a teenager, Maine lived in Los Angeles before settling in Erie, Colorado in the 1990s, where he’s lived since, raising his family and working as an engineer. Over the past three decades, Maine has watched Denver change from a small "cow town" into a large municipality, and witnessed a corresponding political shift as the population boomed. BERNIE SANDERS, DSA REVEAL DEMANDS FOR DEM PARTY AFTER SOCIALISTS SWEEP NEW YORK ELECTIONS "All of a sudden, it wasn't, 'Can we have the smallest government possible and leave us alone?' It became, 'Well, we need to give you free stuff.' And that's when I started to worry a little bit," Maine said. Maine isn't surprised that veteran Democrats are facing primary threats from the far left, noting that Kiros’ campaign benefited from a well-organized ground game and sweeping promises on healthcare and affordability that drew in younger voters. "She is winning the primary because we have an organized group convincing people that they can have free stuff. You can have free medical care. You can have free supermarkets. You can have free transportation. And it's very appealing," Maine explained. "I like free stuff, but what they forget to tell you is that nothing is really free. As they say, there's no free lunch." SOCIALIST HOUSE CANDIDATE SAYS HE AGREES WITH REPUBLICANS ON 'ONE ISSUE' He believes historical lessons are being lost as generations grow further removed from the realities of the Soviet Union. "So there is a gap that's being exploited," he continued. "And it's been exploited from internal and from external, because there's a lot of evil forces in the world that do not want America to succeed." While critics view the rise of the DSA as a dangerous departure from American values, Kiros and other DSA candidates argue their policies are a pragmatic response to liberal voters fed up with how the Democratic Party has responded to their struggles. Kiros recently brushed aside concerns regarding communists inside the DSA faction of the Democratic Party, telling PBS’s "Firing Line" host Margaret Hoover that there is room in the party for various viewpoints. "Yeah. Well, some members of the Democratic Party are proudly proclaiming themselves as capitalists, and it’s a big tent, right?" Kiros said. "But again, at the end of the day, it’s up to the voters, right?" "Until a self-proclaimed communist actually wins an election, then it’s just noise from the Republican Party. There’s no one who’s actually winning with that," she continued. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE Kiros denied being a communist herself, arguing that younger voters are embracing the DSA message because, at its core, it represents "economic populism." Her campaign centered on Medicare for all, universal childcare, investments in public housing, higher federal taxes on the wealthy, publicly owned utilities and more. Like many other socialist campaigns across the country, she is also firmly anti-Israel. Kiros' campaign was backed by several progressive groups, including the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), Justice Democrats, and the Working Families Party. Republican candidate Christy Peterson, a local accountant, is also running in the Nov. 3 general election, which Kiros is widely expected to win given the district's strongly blue lean. In 2024, Kamala Harris won 77 percent of the vote in the district en route to winning Colorado. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Kiros’s campaign and the DSA did not respond to Fox News Digital’s request for comment.
news.summary: A veteran Colorado political insider warned the Democratic Socialists' rise in Denver mirrors the MAGA movement and could become a cancer for Democrats.

news.title: Democratic Candidates Have A New Strategy To Contest Tough Elections – Drop Out
news.text:
As Democrats see President Donald Trump’s popularity sink and their chances for a wave election rise in certain Republican-leaning states, they’re relying on an unusual strategy: Get their own candidates to drop out. 

The strategy follows previous efforts by Democrats to clear the field for independent candidates to run against Republicans in states where the national party brand has become an albatross around their candidates’ necks. And so far, Democratic candidates are getting out of the way in most states — Senate candidates in Nebraska, Idaho and South Dakota, as well as a House candidate in Alaska, have all dropped their bids in favor of independents.

The main exception is in Montana, where GOP Sen. Steve Daines’ last-minute decision not to run for reelection presents an enticing target. So Democratic leaders are hoping their nominee, Alani Bankhead, will also drop out to make way for Seth Bodnar, the former University of Montana president running as an independent.

“It’s kind of a shit show right now,” said former Sen. Jon Tester, who lost reelection in 2024 and is the last Democrat to hold statewide office in Montana. 

Tester is backing Bodnar and has called on Bankhead, an Air Force veteran with little political experience, to withdraw from the race, although he said that he isn’t doing anything behind the scenes to pressure her ahead of the Aug. 10 filing deadline, when she still has a chance to remove her name from the ballot.

But there is an ongoing push to get Bankhead to exit the race, even though she has declared that she will “never drop out” and has said Bodnar should do so instead. 

Bodnar and Bankhead have met in recent days to no avail, according to local media reports. An outside group called Montana Freedom PAC spent more than $1 million on ads and text messages to boost Bodnar and attack Bankhead in July, and is reportedly now distributing lawn signs explicitly calling on Bankhead to withdraw. The state’s chapter of the Service Employees International Union and the Montana Federation of Public Employees, both reliable backers of Democrats, endorsed Bodnar in August.

Lawyers both in the state and from the national Democratic Party law firm Elias Group have presented legal opinions that would allow the party to not replace Bankhead were she to withdraw.

A flurry of polls from Contours, Inc., an organization backing independent candidates including Bodnar, have shown Bodnar leading GOP candidate Kurt Alme in a head-to-head match-up, while Alme easily wins if Bankhead stays in and splits the vote. Other polls have shown Bodnar doing significantly better than Bankhead in head-to-head match-ups with Alme. (Republicans, who would like to keep both candidates in the race, are touting an internal memo from Senate Leadership Fund, the chief super PAC for Senate Republicans, claiming that Bankhead is a stronger candidate than Bodnar.)

“The independent’s got a shot just like in a lot of other states if the Democrat gets out,” Tester said. “Alani Bankhead has lived in the state a quick minute. She has no shot.”

“Alani Bankhead is the Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, and she is staying in this race through November,” Jeri Bucy, director of strategic communications for the Bankhead campaign, said in a statement. “Montana Democrats vetted Alani and chose her in the primary. Seth Bodnar has never been on a ballot or vetted by a single voter. Alani has been direct that the way to beat Kurt Alme is to unite behind the nominee Montanans chose. That’s where our focus is.”

The states where Democrats are looking to back independent candidates are ripe for this particular strategy, according to a study by the political data site Split Ticket. They all have extremely high populations of white people, relatively low populations of evangelicals and high support for Republican candidates. This combination of factors makes an independent candidate viable because they can appeal to voters who wouldn’t vote for a Democrat (white voters) but who aren’t constrained by extreme partisanship (evangelical voters) — all without worrying about alienating Democrats who view their partisanship as part of their personal identity (non-white voters).

And although Montana remains a sore spot, the pressure campaigns have been successful in other states that have not favored Democrats in recent years.

In Nebraska, Democratic Senate nominee Cindy Burbank ended her campaign on July 18 to make way for independent Dan Osborn, a former union leader and Navy veteran who ran a close race against Republican Sen. Deb Fischer in 2024 and is now running against GOP Sen. Pete Ricketts.

Idaho Democratic Senate candidate David Roth ended his bid on July 28, citing a desire to focus his “time and energy on helping Democrats win up and down the ballot and in communities across Idaho.” That leaves former state legislator and Army veteran Todd Achilles, who previously held office as a Democrat but is now running as an independent, as the lone challenger to Republican Sen. Jim Risch.

Roth faced pressure from state Democrats to drop out. Former Democratic Rep. Larry LaRocco wrote op-eds calling for his withdrawal, and the Ada County Democrats threatened to endorse Achilles if Roth could not show that he could raise sufficient funds to compete.

In South Dakota, Democratic Senate nominee Julian Beaudion dropped out on Aug. 4 to clear the path for independent Brian Bengs, a Navy veteran who ran as a Democrat in 2022. Local and national Democrats had been pushing hard for Beaudion to drop his campaign against Republican Sen. Mike Rounds.

Prior to Beaudion’s departure, he faced calls from Steve Hildebrand, a former top aide to ex-Senate Majority Leader Tom Daschle, one of the last Democrats elected statewide in South Dakota, to withdraw and let Bengs run one-on-one against Rounds.

“Let’s be adults. Let’s pretend like we actually care about democracy and not about a candidate. So shut down South Dakota,” Hildebrand said about Beaudion. “Go raise national money, Brian Bengs, and beat the hell out of Rounds using his own votes, and maybe you got a shot. That’s the path to victory in my mind. If you don’t wanna do that, then let’s all go home.”

Alaska Democratic House candidate Matt Schultz dropped his challenge to GOP Rep. Nick Begich on July 17 and endorsed independent Bill Hill, a commercial fisherman and retired school superintendent.

Not all Democrats are fans of pushing out their own candidates, but there is a strong case for it — especially in certain states. It has been more than a decade since a Democrat held a Senate seat in either Nebraska or South Dakota. Montana has gone from having two Democratic senators and a Democratic governor in 2014 to being a solidly Republican state where Democrats struggle at the statewide level. Meanwhile, the last Democrat to represent Idaho in the Senate was Frank Church, who lost his reelection bid in 1980.

But in Nebraska, Osborn came within 6 percentage points of the incumbent, Fischer, in 2024. That margin outpaced Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris by 15 points in the state — the highest differential by any candidate challenging a Republican.

This follows a pattern of independents gaining some ground where Democrats stand down. In Utah, former Republican Trump critic Evan McMullin ran for Senate as an independent in deep-red Utah in 2022 and lost to GOP Sen. Mike Lee by just 10 points. Trump won Utah by 20 points in 2020. In Kansas, where no Democrat has won a Senate race since Herbert Hoover was president, independent Greg Orman lost to then-Sen. Pat Roberts, a Republican, by 11 points in 2014, far outpacing President Barack Obama’s 22-point loss to Mitt Romney in the 2012 presidential election in the state.

And then there’s Alaska, where the state Democratic Party has fully embraced aligning with independent candidates to win elections. This strategy not only helped elect Republican-turned-independent Bill Walker as governor in 2014, but it has led Democrats to form a coalition of independents and moderate Republicans to control both chambers of the state legislature.

Democrats backing independents may not lead to victories in all — or any — of these races. But it could force Republicans to spend money in states that they otherwise wouldn’t bother with, draining their resources in more purple states with tighter races.

For users of the US version of TikTok, the video now carries a message stating that the copyright owner has not made the sound available in their country. The August video is not the only Trump-related TikTok featuring Taylor Swift's music to have lost its audio. A Team Trump video posted on November 6, 2025, which featured Swift's Father Figure, has also had its sound removed. Several other major artists have previously objected to their songs being played at Trump campaign events or used in political messaging. news.title: State lawmaker Tram Nguyen also running as outsider in 6th District
news.text:
The dynamic has largely bifurcated the field into political insiders running with varying levels of establishment backing and those running as status-quo-busting change agents, promising to bring fresh energy to D.C. 

All, however, appear to be emphasizing their pugnacious chops for either sparring with Trump — or with other Democrats.

“The challenge, particularly for candidates that don’t have the same level of resources as [some], is how do you get that message out and how do you turn enough of a vote to get you first over the finish line on Sept. 1,” said Drew Russo, a former aide to John Tierney, the former Sixth District congressman who lost in 2014 to the current departing incumbent, Representative Seth Moulton. 

“Democratic primary voters,” he added, “are showing around the country that they want somebody that’s going to show fight.”

The field includes Dan Koh, a former Boston City Hall and White House aide from Andover who has raised $4.5 million for his bid and leaned heavily into his Washington experience, touting endorsements from Biden and former Vice President Kamala Harris. The former president is included in a mini-montage in Koh’s first television ad, and in another spot, even shows up in a framed photo in Koh’s home.

Former Boston mayor and US Labor Secretary Martin J. Walsh, for whom Koh worked in both D.C. and Boston, has also organized support for him.

“I dedicated my life to public service,” Koh says in one ad.

Others are playing up their nonpolitical backgrounds. John Beccia, a businessman from Lynnfield, has put $3 million of his own money into his campaign. He calls himself the only candidate who has “actually built something” and has promised to back term limits. In campaign mailers, Beccia also criticized unnamed “career politicians.”

Then there’s Tram Nguyen, a state representative from Andover who appears to be marketing herself as a bit of both: She’s a refugee who came from the humblest of beginnings but also talks about being an elected official who gets how the system works and is backed by some of the state’s most powerful legislators to boot.

A former attorney at Greater Boston Legal Services, Nguyen mixes her pitch of Trump resistance into her background as an immigrant who flipped a seat held by a Trump-aligned Republican, becoming the first Vietnamese American woman elected to public office in Massachusetts.

Her campaign website includes a section that mimics a so-called red box, a kind of information alert that candidates use to get around federal rules that bar direct coordination with outside groups such as super PACs. The boxes typically suggest what type of messaging those groups can use to support that candidate.

In Nguyen’s case, the section on her website simultaneously emphasizes her background as an “effective State Representative” and an “outsider.” 

“There are some unique elements to her personal story and her professional background that are compelling to a lot of people,” said Matt Chilliak, chair of the Andover Democratic Town Committee who is not publicly supporting a candidate.

“But,” he added, “I would not describe her professional background as being an outsider.”

Nguyen said in an interview that while the “legislative role is the same” between state government and Congress, the two positions are also “very different.”

“I’m not looking to go to D.C. to be a part of the establishment,” she said. “I’m looking to fix it.”

She’s not the only candidate to emphasize bringing a new or outside perspective to Washington. Bethany Andres-Beck, a Middleton software engineer, has similarly leaned on their background in technology to argue that federal policies on subjects such as artificial intelligence should be shaped by people who have scientific or technical expertise and not solely a political background.

Two other candidates, Jamie Belsito of Topsfield and Mariah Lancaster, a former federal worker and veterinarian from Salem, have pledged to upend the status quo in Congress while also referencing work with local and federal government.

Belsito, a former state representative, has worked on federal abortion policy, and Lancaster is a former State Department and congressional staffer. They’ve each taken up progressive mantles in their campaigns, often criticizing the mainstream Democratic Party.

To Jonathan Cohn, policy director for Progressive Mass, which is backing Nguyen, candidates are trying anything to distinguish themselves in a race that “has the feeling” of the 2018 primary for the Third Congressional District, located just to the west along the northern Massachusetts border. In that race, a crowded field of Democrats pitched themselves as an antidote to President Trump. (Koh was a candidate in that primary, too, which was won by the current incumbent, Lori Trahan.)

There isn’t any independent polling to show whether any one candidate is breaking through. But internal surveys by the campaigns largely show a closely packed field with many survey takers undecided. (An internal poll released by Koh’s camp Tuesday put him above the pack.)

That has candidates pitching various parts of their resumés in hopes of finding that one angle that will resonate more with Democratic voters.

It has also opened up various lines of attack. Framing Koh as an insider choice — and perhaps indirectly as a front-runner — Beccia and Nguyen have openly prodded the Andover Democrat to debate them, though the candidates have regularly appeared together in forums.

“A debate is the one place in this race that money and influence cannot buy,” Beccia charged.

Belsito, meanwhile, is pitching herself as an “outspoken, unapologetic Democrat” willing to take on those within her own party, including during the year-plus she spent in the Legislature. 

For instance, she has attacked Nguyen’s legislative experience and accused her of being “dishonest about her record,” pointing to a 2024 Globe report that found a legislative committee on climate change that Nguyen received a $22,000 stipend to chair handled few, if any, actual bills. 

Belsito has also accused Nguyen of being beholden to leaders in the Legislature for backing legislation that would narrow state Auditor Diana DiZoglio’s probe of the Legislature. (DiZoglio has endorsed Belsito). A spokesperson for Nguyen, who initially declined to say how she voted on a ballot question allowing DiZoglio to do so, later said she voted against the initiative over “concerns” about its constitutionality.

Nguyen dismissed Belsito’s comments, saying her committee solicited input from environmental stakeholders statewide and conveyed the Legislature’s work to the public.

The race was “not about who yells the loudest at Trump,” she said, “or at each other.”

news.title: Taylor Swift makes brutal swipe after Trump uses 'august' in TikTok
news.text:
Taylor Swift has stripped the audio from a Team Trump TikTok video after the account used her song august without asking, effectively shutting down the campaign's ability to use the track on the platform going forward.

The clip, posted by the official @teamtrump account, came with a sarcastic caption claiming the singer would be 'super excited' the campaign had used her music, alongside hashtags including #taylorswift, #maga and #august. 

This isn't the first time Trump's team or the wider White House TikTok presence has used Swift's work without a formal blessing. 

Within a short space of time, the sound had been muted, meaning anyone watching the video now sees the footage with no audio at all.

Her track The Fate of Ophelia reportedly soundtracked a White House TikTok post earlier this year, and imagery from her Eras Tour was used in content marking America's 250th birthday. 

Neither of those instances resulted in the audio or footage being pulled.

Why can Taylor Swift block songs on TikTok when other artists can't?

The reason Swift can act this fast comes down to ownership. Unlike most major artists, she owns both her masters and her publishing rights, having bought back her back catalogue after a lengthy and very public dispute with her former label. That dual ownership means she doesn't need permission from a record label or publisher to have a video muted or pulled, she can seemingly make the call herself.

Most musicians who object to politicians using their songs at rallies or online run into a wall of red tape, since rights are often split between labels, publishers and other stakeholders, some of whom may already have licensing arrangements with platforms like TikTok. Swift's setup effectively cuts out the middleman.

Has Taylor Swift spoken out about Donald Trump before?

The singer endorsed Kamala Harris ahead of the 2024 presidential election, and at the time referenced AI-generated images that had circulated showing her appearing to back Trump, which she said played a part in her decision to go public with her endorsement.

There was also the widely-discussed moment where Madison Square Garden's electronic billboards, previously used to mark her engagement to Travis Kelce, were changed to display a message reading 'Trump is your president'.

UNILAD has approached Taylor Swift and The White House for comment.
news.summary: The pair have previously clashed on social media, most recently with a White House post after Taylor Swift's wedding to Travis Kelce

news.title: Taylor Swift Silences Trump on TikTok as President's Team Uses 'Red' to Claim Album Is About the GOP
news.text:
Taylor Swift has appeared to shut down Donald Trump's latest attempt to use her music on social media after a Team Trump TikTok video featuring her song August was muted, prompting supporters to celebrate what they saw as a quiet response from the singer.

The official Team Trump account uploaded the video on Monday, showing President Donald Trump and First Lady Melania Trump watching fireworks while celebrating his presidency. The post used Swift's 2020 hit August as its soundtrack and included the caption, 'I'm sure Taylor Swift is going to be super excited we used her song.'

Hours later, however, viewers noticed the music had disappeared. In its place was TikTok's standard copyright notice stating, 'The copyright owner hasn't made this sound available in your country.'

Neither Swift, TikTok nor the Trump campaign has publicly explained why the audio became unavailable, and IBTimes UK cannot independently verify whether the change resulted from a copyright claim, licensing restrictions or another platform-related issue.

Team Trump Uses Taylor Swift Song Despite Political Divide

The TikTok video appeared to deliberately reference Swift's long-running political opposition to Trump. Overlaying footage of the president and first lady watching fireworks was the text, 'Mood because it's August and Donald Trump is your president.'

Using August was notable given Swift's public support for Democratic candidates in recent election cycles. She endorsed Joe Biden and Kamala Harris in 2020 before backing Harris again during the 2024 presidential race.

The campaign appeared aware of the political irony, acknowledging it directly in the caption accompanying the upload. Although politicians have frequently used popular music during campaigns, artists have also repeatedly objected to their work being associated with political messaging they do not support.

Muted Audio Sparks Online Celebration

Once the soundtrack disappeared, Swift fans quickly interpreted the move as a victory. Comments across TikTok and X celebrated what many believed was Swift reclaiming control over her music.

One user wrote, 'TAYLOR REMOVING THE AUDIO.' Another replied, 'QUEEEEN.' Others joked that the singer had 'deleted the song' from the campaign's post.

While many fans assumed Swift or her representatives had intervened, there is currently no public evidence confirming that was the case. TikTok routinely removes audio when licensing agreements or rights restrictions apply, and the precise reason behind the change remains unclear.

Team Trump Responds With 'Red'

Rather than moving on from the episode, Team Trump leaned further into the online conversation. The campaign later uploaded another TikTok using Swift's song Red, joking that the album had always represented the Republican Party's signature colour.

The caption claimed, 'Did you know Taylor Swift wrote a whole album about the color of the Republican Party.' The video also rewrote several of Swift's song titles to fit Republican messaging.

Among the altered titles were Everything Has Changed to Everything Has Changed (At Our Southern Border), and The Last Time to The Last Time (An Autopen Runs the Country). The follow-up post suggested the campaign intended to keep the exchange alive rather than avoid the backlash.

A Long-Running Political Feud

The latest TikTok exchange adds another chapter to the increasingly public relationship between Trump and one of the world's biggest pop stars. Swift largely avoided political endorsements during the early years of her career before becoming increasingly outspoken in recent elections.

Trump has repeatedly criticised the singer over those endorsements. Following Swift's support for Kamala Harris during the 2024 campaign, Trump told reporters, 'I was not a Taylor Swift fan. It was just a question of time.'

He added, 'She's a very liberal person, she seems to always endorse a Democrat and she'll probably pay a price for it in the marketplace.' Those remarks became one of several public exchanges between the president and the Grammy-winning artist.

Politics, Copyright and Internet Culture Collide

The incident highlights how political campaigns increasingly rely on recognisable pop culture references to generate attention online. Whether the disappearance of August resulted from a copyright restriction or a routine licensing issue, the muted soundtrack quickly became part of the story itself.

For Swift's supporters, it was viewed as a subtle rejection of the campaign's attempt to associate itself with her music. For Team Trump, the follow-up use of Red suggested the campaign was content to continue provoking one of its most prominent celebrity critics. Neither Swift nor representatives for Trump had publicly commented on the muted TikTok audio at the time of publication.

Until either side explains what happened, the reason the song disappeared remains uncertain. What is clear is that a single muted soundtrack has become the latest flashpoint in the long-running political divide between Donald Trump and Taylor Swift, a dispute that continues to play out as much on social media as it does on the campaign trail.

news.title: The loss of TPS brings another humiliation for Haitians — ankle monitors
news.text:
SPRINGFIELD, Ohio – The long-feared loss of their temporary protected status means hundreds of thousands of Haitian immigrants in the United States are days into a new reality of knowing they could be deported at any time.

And until they are, many must cope with having to wear an ankle monitor issued by the Department of Homeland Security — a piece of surveillance technology that has become a fact of life for an increasing number of people in the United States now without legal residency.

After the Supreme Court allowed the Trump administration to end TPS for Haitians, Immigration and Customs Enforcement personnel began requiring the monitors for those in Springfield, Ohio, long a scapegoat for the administration. Another judge made that ruling official Wednesday by lifting an order that blocked the administration from moving ahead. 

Although ankle monitors have been deployed for decades on those involved in immigration proceedings, the Trump administration is aggressively expanding the use of the devices, which are more commonly associated with people charged with crimes or out on parole.

In 2025, ICE awarded a contract worth up to $1 billion to BI Inc., a Boulder, Colorado-based manufacturer of GPS-enabled ankle monitors and other “detention alternatives” and a provider of monitoring services. That followed a multiyear contract worth $2.2 billion awarded in 2020 to BI, a subsidiary of the GEO Group, one of the nation’s largest private detention firms.

In June 2025, under then-Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem, ICE ordered its field officers to slap ankle monitors on immigrants “whenever possible,” a departure from longstanding policies such as using app or voice check-ins, even though at least one study has questioned their effectiveness in immigration settings.

As a result, over 30% of the more than 183,000 people ICE monitored on an average day in the past fiscal year using “alternative to detention” methods were forced to wear an ankle or wrist monitor, up from 18% the previous year.

In fiscal 2025, people in the program showed up for court appearances 98.2% of the time, a number that actually dipped very slightly the following year as the use of ankle monitors went up. (Those figures aren’t broken down by the type of monitoring, and the percentage of people who showed up for their final deportation hearings went from 86.4% to 91.1%, according to ICE data sourced from BI.)

BI did not immediately respond Friday to MS NOW’s request for comment on its government contracts.

It’s estimated that 330,000 to 350,000 Haitians in the U.S. previously held TPS. In Springfield alone, the diaspora is estimated to be around 12,000. Many of them received letters from DHS in recent days calling them to an ICE field office in Blue Ash, Ohio, about an hour away.

As they emerged last Sunday with monitors around their ankles, they were enveloped by hundreds of demonstrators protesting the administration’s actions.

“They’re very much ashamed of the ankle monitors,” said Viles Dorsainvil, the executive director of the Haitian Support Center in Springfield who escorted those summoned to the ICE facility in Blue Ash.

“When they get home with them, they’re ashamed to show that to their kids because they’re not criminals,” said Dorsainvil, who connects Haitians in Springfield to legal, interpreter and mental health services.

For people who are in immigration court proceedings, it’s not new for ICE to force them at check-ins to choose between an ankle monitor or being detained, said Rebecca Bundy, the supervising attorney at Advocates for Basic Legal Equality, or ABLE, in Toledo.

“However, for many folks in the Haitian community … these are not people who are in immigration court proceedings. They are people who filed affirmative asylum applications with USCIS, and so the jurisdiction and the procedure is completely different,” she said. 

“We’re actually not sure yet how the immigration enforcement, CBP, and ICE are claiming to have the authority to impose these restrictions, impose the ankle monitor,” Bundy added. 

MS NOW reached out to DHS about its ankle monitor policy, including whether officers are following the same policy in other Haitian American enclaves. DHS didn’t comment on the monitors specifically, instead quoting a song by the band “Semisonic.” 

“It’s closing time which means you don’t have to go home, but you can’t stay here. The good news is it’s not too late to get a $2,600 check and a free flight home,” a DHS spokesperson said in a statement. 

Trump notoriously targeted the Haitian community in Springfield on the debate stage against then-Vice President Kamala Harris in the fall of 2024, greatly amplifying an unfounded rumor that had been confined to smaller corners of social media.

The DHS letters and ankle monitor tactics have Haitian leaders in Springfield worried about the mental health of their community. 

“I’m worried a lot about self-harm and strokes because some of them tell me they got that letter and they haven’t slept,” said Annette Huelskamp, a 38-year-old Haitian American volunteering at the Haitian Support Center in Springfield.

James Fleurijean is the administrative assistant at the Haitian Support Center and a former TPS holder himself who volunteers his time while also being at risk of deportation. He said the ankle monitor policy is “humiliating,” serving as an ever-present reminder of the threat of deportation to a place still so overrun by gangs that the U.S. State Department lists it as a “do not travel” country, its highest warning level, “due to the risk of crime, kidnapping, terrorism, unrest, and limited health care.”

Fleurijean said the letters and ankle monitors are having a devastating toll on the community, but they somehow persevere.

“That’s what keeps me going,” he said.

The follow-up post suggested the campaign intended to keep the exchange alive rather than avoid the backlash.A Long-Running Political FeudThe latest TikTok exchange adds another chapter to the increasingly public relationship between Trump and one of the world's biggest pop stars. Swift largely avoided political endorsements during the early years of her career before becoming increasingly outspoken in recent elections.Trump has repeatedly criticised the singer over those endorsements. Following Swift's support for Kamala Harris during the 2024 campaign, Trump told reporters, 'I was not a Taylor Swift fan. It was just a question of time.'He added, 'She's a very liberal person, she seems to always endorse a Democrat and she'll probably pay a price for it in the marketplace.' Those remarks became one of several public exchanges between the president and the Grammy-winning artist.Politics, Copyright and Internet Culture CollideThe incident highlights how political campaigns increasingly rely on recognisable pop culture references to generate attention online. Whether the disappearance of August resulted from a copyright restriction or a routine licensing issue, the muted soundtrack quickly became part of the story itself.For Swift's supporters, it was viewed as a subtle rejection of the campaign's attempt to associate itself with her music. For Team Trump, the follow-up use of Red suggested the campaign was content to continue provoking one of its most prominent celebrity critics. Neither Swift nor representatives for Trump had publicly commented on the muted TikTok audio at the time of publication.Until either side explains what happened, the reason the song disappeared remains uncertain. What is clear is that a single muted soundtrack has become the latest flashpoint in the long-running political divide between Donald Trump and Taylor Swift, a dispute that continues to play out as much on social media as it does on the campaign trail.

news.title: Taylor Swift's 'August' removed from Donald Trump's campaign TikTok video
news.text:
Washington DC [US], August 8 (ANI) : A TikTok video that included Taylor Swift's song "August" posted four days ago to the account for US President Donald Trump 's campaign has had the sound removed, according to Variety. The video, posted four days ago by the official @TeamTrump TikTok account, featured Trump and Melania Trump standing on a balcony and watching fireworks. The text over the video read, "Mood because it's August and Donald Trump is your president."Its caption originally read, "I'm sure @Taylor Swift is going to be super excited we used her song! #taylorswift #maga #august."Fans noticed that Swift's "August", from her 2020 album Folklore, had been removed from the video. In the US version of TikTok, a message displayed on the post says: "The copyright owner hasn't made this sound available in your country," according to Variety. One of the top comments on the video reacted to the removal, with a user writing: "TAYLOR REMOVING THE AUDIO QUEEEEEEN."

The @TeamTrump TikTok account, which has around 14 million followers, was created ahead of the 2024 US presidential election and has continued to post videos regularly since Trump returned to the White House for a second term, as per the outlet. This is not the first Trump campaign TikTok featuring Swift's music to lose its audio. A Team Trump video featuring Swift's song "Father Figure", posted on November 6, 2025, has also had its audio removed.However, a Team Trump video posted a day ago featuring a version of Swift's "Red" still had its audio track available as of the time of reporting. A video posted on the official White House TikTok account last November also continues to feature Swift's "The Fate of Ophelia".Swift and Trump have previously clashed publicly over politics. In September 2024, Trump posted "I HATE TAYLOR SWIFT!" on social media after the singer announced her support for then-Democratic presidential candidate Kamala Harris, according to Variety. "I'm voting for @kamalaharris because she fights for the rights and causes I believe need a warrior to champion them," Swift had written in an Instagram post.The dispute followed another controversy in August 2024, when Trump shared AI-generated images falsely suggesting that Swift had endorsed him for president. One image depicted Swift as Uncle Sam alongside a message reading, "Taylor wants you to vote for Donald Trump," as per the outlet. At the time, Trump suggested in an interview with Fox Business that he was not concerned about Swift suing him over the fabricated images, saying they "were all made up by other people." (ANI)

news.title: Jill Biden admits she doesn’t think America will have a woman president in her lifetime
news.text:
Jill Biden has admitted she does not expect to see a woman become president of the United States during her lifetime.

The former first lady, now 75, was asked about the prospect during an appearance on SiriusXM’s Let’s Talk Off Camera with Kelly Ripa, as the conversation turned to the country’s long wait to elect a woman to the White House.

America has had women serve as vice president, run major presidential campaigns, and secure nominations from a major party, but the top job has remained out of reach.

Biden, who spent four years in the White House whilst her husband Joe was president, has previously campaigned alongside some of the most prominent women in Democratic politics.

With all that in mind, her latest comments suggest she is far less confident about seeing that final barrier broken than she once was.

Her pessimism appears to stem from the 2024 election, when she believed Kamala Harris was on course to win.

Asked whether she thought they would ever see a woman president, as noted by People, Jill replied: “In my lifetime. I’m 75. I feel like probably not in my lifetime, Kelly, but maybe in yours.”

She then explained just how strongly she had expected Harris to make history after replacing Joe Biden at the top of the Democratic ticket.

She continued: “I really did think last time that Kamala was gonna win. I was out on the campaign trail for her,

“I saw the excitement, I saw the crowds, I saw [it] at the convention. I saw all the energy, and I thought, ‘Finally, we’re going to have a woman president.’ And I must tell you, I was shocked... the morning after when I got up at 5:00 in the morning to feed Willow and get ready for the day, and I found out that she had lost. Shocked.”

Harris became the Democratic nominee after Joe Biden ended his re-election campaign in July 2024, following intense pressure after his debate performance against Donald Trump.

She ultimately lost the election to Trump, although talk of another possible White House run has continued.

Harris, New York Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, and Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer are among the Democratic women whose names have been discussed as candidates to potentially stand in the 2028 presidential election.

Jill is also not the only former first lady to express doubts about America electing a woman. Noted by Fox News, Michelle Obama previously told an audience that the country ‘ain’t ready’ after Harris’ defeat, prompting disagreement from other high-profile Democrats.

Harris herself rejected that idea in an interview with The New York Times in December 2025, saying: “I do believe the country is ready.”

Former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi also pushed back when asked about Obama’s comments, questioning why a woman should be considered unable to serve as commander-in-chief.

She said: "Well, I hope — I mean, I respect her and I know that view is one that we all are saddened by, but we — I think we have to change. The fact is that I‘ve heard every excuse in the book, you know, like, 'I‘m not sure a woman could be commander-in-chief.' Well, why not?" she asked.

"'Well, I served in the military.' Well, OK. And so? So do women serve in the military."
news.summary: Kamala Harris’ 2024 defeat changed how Jill Biden sees America’s political future
news.author: Ben Williams

news.title: El-Sayed ran an arrogant campaign. Now he wants unity?
news.text:
Abdul El-Sayed won the Democratic nomination for Michigan Senate, but by much less than anticipated. After weeks of running an arrogant campaign that alienated Rep. Haley Stevens' voters, his campaign is now pivoting to unity.

The irony is that for years the progressive wing of the Democratic Party, including El-Sayed, has made it clear their vote cannot be counted on when moderates win.

Moderate Democrats are asked to unify behind candidates they dislike and don't get the same grace when they win. Democrats can only expect more of these heated primaries to further fracture their party.

El-Sayed was expected to win big in the weeks leading up to the primary, and he ran his campaign like it. Instead, he won by less than a percentage point. Rather than bring the other side into the fold, he treated Stevens and her supporters as if he didn't need their votes, or as if their concerns with his candidacy didn't matter.

"She votes to send our money abroad while Michiganders struggle," El-Sayed said of Stevens on X July 17. "She's bought by DTE (Energy), Blue Cross, Big Tech, and Big Pharma who pick our pockets."

Ironically, that rhetoric was part of a message meant to rein in unkind personal attacks from his supporters against Stevens, but that doesn't make it any less divisive. El-Sayed also called her "the least capable candidate in America" during another podcast appearance.

Abdul El-Sayed calls for unity now that he needs Haley Stevens' voters

That kind of rhetoric is extremely divisive for someone who won his primary by less than a point and didn't even win a majority of the vote. Compare it with how El-Sayed talks about Stevens now that he needs the support of her voters in November.

"She is one of the most committed public servants that you'll ever meet. She loves democracy, like I love democracy," El-Sayed said of Stevens on Aug. 5, after his victory. "Whatever differences that we might have had in the primary, they pale in comparison to what unifies us."

El-Sayed's campaign surrogates have made the situation even worse for him. Hasan Piker, the antisemitic Twitch streamer and friend of El-Sayed, dismissed anyone acknowledging El-Sayed has work to do mending bridges as "unbelievably Islamophobic pieces of s---."

Even if El-Sayed wasn't already a divisive candidate, his campaign proxies are only driving a further wedge between him and the moderate Democrats he needs to win in November.

If Stevens won, would El-Sayed give her the same benefit?

Both Stevens and El-Sayed have made a concerted effort at amends now that the primary is over. The two rivals hugged on stage at the Michigan Democrats' "unity breakfast," an event planned before the primary had even ended. 

The Michigan primary was uniquely contentious and was the most expensive Democratic Senate primary in history.

However, I'm not so sure Democrats could have expected the same unity had the outcome been flipped. El-Sayed and his base have a history of undermining establishment candidates once they win the nomination.

In the 2024 election, El-Sayed was a loud advocate for the "uncommitted" movement, which urged Democratic voters upset with Israel's military actions in Gaza to vote uncommitted in the presidential primary.

Although El-Sayed later endorsed Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris after President Joe Biden dropped out, and the organizers of uncommitted ultimately urged supporters to "vote against" Donald Trump, the movement had already done its damage.

Trump went on to win Dearborn, Michigan's majority-Muslim district, due in part to the fact that 20% of voters there cast their ballot for someone other than Trump or Harris. He also carried Michigan statewide, a state Democrats had counted on and could ill afford to lose. 

Compare that with 2020, when Biden won nearly 75% of the vote in Dearborn and Michigan overall.

El-Sayed still can't extend an olive branch to moderates, and holds the same arrogant attitude looking ahead.

"I'm happy to show you around so long as you want to get money out of politics, put money in our pocket and pass Medicare for all," El-Sayed said of potential 2028 presidential candidates visiting Michigan. "If not, I'm going to dog you up and down the state." 

That's how someone who won a landslide talks when they want to be a political kingmaker, not how a plurality primary winner should sound.

Democrats may be comfortable with these contentious primaries as they work through their soul-searching as a party. But any compromises moderates make to back progressive candidates shouldn't be expected in return when the results go the other way.

Dace Potas is an opinion columnist for USA TODAY and a graduate of DePaul University with a degree in political science.
